name: Gorillas Direct
approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls. For the Cascadian Couloir and South Headwall, turn right onto the Longs Pass Trail at the junction about 1.7 miles in, climb to Longs Pass (about 6,250 ft) near mile 2.9, and descend the rocky climbers' trail on the far side to Ingalls Creek, cross on a log bridge, and follow the climbers' path up the meadow into the base of the Cascadian Couloir (South Headwall lies further up-basin via the same drainage). For West Ridge, the North Ridge routes, and the West Face Wall (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), instead stay on the Ingalls Way Trail over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3) and continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft) — the West Face Wall with the Gorillas routes sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, while West Ridge and North Ridge climbers continue over or along Goat Pass toward their respective start points. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek depending on the objective. The North Ridge routes can also be reached from the opposite (Mountaineer Creek) side.
descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend via the main gully with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right on a large bench with a single-rope rappel option, before reaching Stuart Pass bivy sites.
hazards: Loose rock and dirt on the upper mountain, particularly on the final traverse back right above the headwall

waysIn.name: Ingalls Lake to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass
waysIn.season: Roughly late Jul-early Sep, once the snow below the wall has gone down enough to reach the start by a short scramble and before autumn storms
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then take the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge.

The wall these routes are on sits in the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, rising about 1,000 ft out of the snow. It is known as the West Face Wall — worth saying plainly, because it faces west and some descriptions of the mountain's south side sweep it in with the south face, which sends parties looking on the wrong aspect.

Bivy sites are at Stuart Pass and at Goat Pass. Most parties camp at one of them and walk in to the wall in the morning.

The descent goes over the top: continue up the West Ridge to the summit, or take the main West Ridge gully down with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right onto a large bench where a single-rope rappel gets you back toward the Stuart Pass bivies.
hazards: Snow at the foot of the wall early in the season, making the short scramble to the start awkward
Long runouts between placements and hidden loose chockstones
A west-facing wall that gets full afternoon sun and afternoon weather
Topping out high on the West Ridge with a long descent still to do
An unplanned bivy is a real outcome; parties carry for it

name: Standard Scramble (from Foggy Lake)
approach: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway (19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center), on the Weeden Creek Trail / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724). The first ~0.7 mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing steadily through forest; the trail fords Weeden Creek around the 1.1-mile mark (no bridge — the main reliable water source low on the route). From there the trail switchbacks up a steep, root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft/mile through a roughly 2-mile crux band; this section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche run-out debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy-snow years, and can require an ice axe. Around 3.5–4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin (around 5,000 ft) — the last dependable water before the final push and a good bail-out point in poor weather. From the basin, continue up talus and slab benches roughly another 0.5–0.6 mile to the saddle above Foggy Lake (total to the lake is about 9.2 miles / 2,800–3,100 ft round trip per multiple trail sources), then drop slightly and traverse roughly 0.3–0.4 mile along/above the lake's shore to its outlet. At the outlet, leave the maintained tread for an intermittent, cairned climber's path onto Gothic Peak's SE ridge; stay in the scree climber's-right of the ridge crest rather than on the crest itself, following cairns past a small tarn at the base of a snowfield and up broken rock to the base of the summit block. Route-finding is the main approach-specific hazard: in early season, snow can bury the cairned line, and many parties inadvertently stray onto exposed Class 4 rock to climber's-left of the correct, easier line just below the summit block.
descent: Reverse the ascent line — the correct SE-ridge descent is generally easier to pick out looking downhill than it was on the way up, and most parties who wandered onto the harder Class 4 rock on the ascent spot the easier Class 3 bypass ('sidewalk' ledge) on the way down. From the true summit, downclimb the short (~100 vertical foot) summit block via its broken south-side terrain rather than traversing climber's-left, which dead-ends above the exposed south face in sustained 4th-class ground. Continue down the scree/talus on the north side of the SE ridge crest (the climber's-right side on the way up) back to the Foggy Lake outlet on the same cairned line used on the ascent, then retrace the maintained Gothic Basin trail — through the basin meadows, the steep timbered switchback band, and the Weeden Creek ford — back to the Barlow Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling required in normal summer conditions. The real hazards are loose rock and fall exposure on the summit block and upper scree, and, in early-season or wet/icy conditions, hard snow on the slabs and snowfield just below the ridge, where an ice axe (and caution on the creek crossing) is warranted. A short handline is occasionally carried by conservative parties for the final summit-block downclimb, but it is not standard gear for this route. In early July, an easier but chossy class 2 alternative leaves the base of the summit block and drops to climber's left below the ridge; it crosses a moderate-angle snow traverse that month.
hazards: steep, loose rock gully just below the summit block — rockfall risk increases with more parties on route
short, exposed class 3–4 scrambling on the final ~150 ft summit block
small moat between snow and rock near the summit block late in the season
persistent fog and low cloud common in Gothic Basin, complicating route-finding on the ridge
snow bridges and avalanche debris runouts possible on the approach trail into early summer; basin/gullies can hold snow into early September in heavy-snow years
no reliable cell coverage east of the Verlot Public Service Center
very heavy weekend foot and camping traffic on a highly popular trail/scramble

waysIn.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake outlet
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; cairns can be buried by snow into early summer
waysIn.notes:
Distance is round trip to Foggy Lake. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, about 19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center, on the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724).

The first two thirds of a mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing through forest. The trail fords Weden Creek at around 1.1 miles — no bridge, and the main reliable water low on the route. Above that it switchbacks up a steep root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft per mile through a roughly two-mile band that is the physical crux of the walk. That section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy years.

At about 3.5 to 4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin — the last dependable water and a sensible bail-out point in bad weather. Continue up talus and slab benches another half mile to the saddle above Foggy Lake, then drop slightly and traverse three or four tenths of a mile along and above the shore to the lake's outlet.
hazards: Snow patches and avalanche debris across the tread in the steep timber band
Weden Creek ford
Buried cairns in early season, leading parties onto exposed class 4 left of the correct line

name: Southeast Slopes (Standard Scramble)
approach: The Southeast Slopes route is approached via the Upper Dungeness/Maynard Burn trail system, not by any direct road-side access - the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120 (off FR-2870/Lost Mountain Rd, itself off Palo Alto Rd south of US-101 near Sequim). From the trailhead, the Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 crosses Mueller Creek right away (the last easy, reliable water for a while) and follows an old roadbed before narrowing to single-track around 0.3 mile in. From there the trail turns and stays steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a bit over 2 miles on tread that narrows to barely a boot-width across eroded, crumbly ravine crossings and packed-dirt/shattered-shale slopes - a legitimate climber's-path pitch, not a graded trail. Around the 2.7-mile mark (about 6,200 ft) the trail tops out on the saddle/ridge crest between Tyler Peak and Baldy; a short, steep side path drops off the ridge here to the last dependable water (snowmelt-fed) before the high traverse. From the saddle it's roughly a mile more, past Pt. 6537, to Baldy's summit (reported as 6,797-6,827 ft). For the Gray Wolf Ridge extension, continue past Baldy: drop about 600 ft off its far side, then follow the long, open, mostly-unmarked ridge crest - packed dirt, shattered shale, and short talus/scree sections - over intermediate high points (including Pt. 7076) to Gray Wolf Peak's 7,218-ft summit, roughly 6-7 miles and up to 7,000 cumulative ft of gain from the trailhead depending on how much re-ascent the ridge undulations add. Because the line stays on or near an exposed above-treeline crest for miles, wind, afternoon thunderstorms, and lingering snow patches into July (which can bury the intermittent boot path and warrant an axe) are the main approach-specific hazards. There is no reliable water once you commit to the ridge crest past the Baldy saddle, so tank up at Mueller Creek and the saddle spring beforehand. Expect to detour briefly around occasional gendarmes and false summits along the ridge crest, and carry a map or GPS since long stretches of the crest are unmarked and off-trail.
descent: The standard descent simply reverses the ascent ridge: back over Pt. 7076 and the connecting crest, back up-and-over Baldy, then down the Upper/Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 to the trailhead. This is a walk/scramble reversal with no technical downclimbing and no rappelling required on the standard line (rappels: 0). A known alternative exists for parties continuing the traverse rather than backtracking: dropping directly off Gray Wolf Ridge's east face into Royal Basin, losing roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail, then exiting via Royal Basin/Dosewalips or looping back to Lower Maynard Burn. This east-face variant is steep, loose, and only lightly traveled - parties describe packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber to find blazes/cairns, with some parties scree-skiing the looser upper sections instead of roping up at all. It is not a bolted or standardized rappel line: where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns/slings, not fixed hardware. Expect at most one or two short rappels (well under 60m each) if a party chooses to rope through a cliff band, rather than a sustained multi-pitch rappel descent - most groups downclimb or scree-ski through instead. Treat this variant as route-finding-dependent and confirm current conditions before relying on it, since little is known about it and there is no fixed, repeatable rappel count.
hazards: Gray Wolf River bridge on the old Gray Wolf Trail route to Baldy is out — that way in needs a hazardous ford; the Maynard Burn approach does not cross the river
loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the ridge crest
sudden, fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on the open, above-treeline ridge
lingering steep snowfields on north-facing gullies into July, requiring an ice axe
long off-trail, unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
black bear and mountain goat encounters — bear canister required within Olympic National Park

waysIn.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
waysIn.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.
hazards: Sudden fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on an open above-treeline ridge with miles of exposure
Loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the crest
Lingering steep snowfields in north-facing gullies into July, warranting an ice axe
No reliable water once past the Baldy saddle spring
Long unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
The Gray Wolf River bridge on the old Gray Wolf Trail route is out — do not plan to come in that way without a hazardous ford
Bear canister required within Olympic National Park

waysIn.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the exit after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.
hazards: Steep, loose, lightly travelled ground with no established line and improvised anchors if roped
Roughly 3,000 ft of descent or ascent on packed dirt and shattered shale
Brushy notches and timber navigation looking for blazes and cairns
Committing: once on the east face there is no easy return to the crest
Every ridge-crest hazard above, in a longer day
waysIn.whyThisWay: When turning the climb into a traverse or loop, finishing down to the Royal Basin trail instead of retracing the Baldy ridge, accepting steep loose ground.

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, Wenatchee River Ranger District), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north, entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles, to Spider Meadow (about 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead). Continue past Spider Meadow on the climbers' path, staying right of the tumbling creek to scramble up slabs past waterfalls, then continue up grass, talus, and heather slopes trending northeast into upper Phelps Basin. A commonly used bivy sits around 5,700-5,800 ft near treeline with stream access (the basin above 6,000 ft often has only snow-patch camping). In upper Phelps Basin the trail fades; in late July staying climbers-left to about 5,800 ft, then turning right toward the main drainage under Dumbell, worked well, and a bootpath beside that gully shows in early September. The access road is rocky, so bring some clearance.
descent: Descend the West Ridge talus back to the Dumbell-Greenwood col, then carefully reverse the narrow connecting ledge around Dumbell's east face to the ~7,900 ft notch above the south-side gully. Downclimb the loose Class 2-3 gully/ledges back into upper Phelps Basin; on snow, plunge-stepping or glissading speeds this section when conditions allow. There is no rappel route commonly described for this line — the ledge and gullies are downclimbed. Do not attempt the ledge crossing in the wet; several parties have retreated rather than cross it in rain.
hazards: The connecting traverse ledge between the Dumbell/Greenwood col and Greenwood's west ridge is roughly a foot wide in places with steep exposure to the east, and one section passes under a small overhang that narrows enough to require crawling.
Early-season parties (through mid-August) encounter moderate snow slopes in the upper basin and on the connecting ledge, requiring an ice axe and crampons.
The final 100 feet of the approach to the 7,900-foot notch on Greenwood's southeast ridge is very loose Class 2+ rock.
Wet or rainy conditions have caused parties to retreat from the exposed ledge traverse rather than cross it.

name: Southeast Route
approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Rd 6024 out of Baring) do not follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055; instead walk back down the access road roughly a quarter mile and pick up the old, deactivated Barclay Creek spur road (parties who know the route often park directly at the spur's gated start rather than the main Barclay Lake lot). Follow the old roadbed about 100-200 yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden 'Gunn climbers' path.' The path drops to Barclay Creek and crosses via a log-jam/rock-hop near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island — this ford is the approach's main early-season hazard, since the crossing can run high and slick with spring runoff. On the far bank the boot path swings west then turns north and starts climbing in earnest: about 200 ft of easier grade gives way to sustained, tight switchbacks gaining roughly 1,500 ft through second-growth timber with generally good tree/root holds underfoot but a steep, sometimes loose tread. Around 3,600-3,800 ft the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, a known route-finding trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band in partial shade. A usually-dry waterfall ravine is crossed around 4,400 ft (can carry meltwater and be slick in early season). The trail continues switchbacking up brushy, sometimes slide-alder-choked terrain for another ~1,500 ft to gain the ridge crest at roughly 5,400 ft — call it 3-4 hours and about 3,200 ft of gain above the creek crossing for a fit party. From the ridge crest, drop about 100 ft off the crest to skirt a cliff band, then boulder-hop roughly 500 ft up a talus basin to the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face, which marks the base of the summit scrambling. There is no reliable water above Barclay Creek/the waterfall ravine in late summer, so fill up early. Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus, so route-finding (not technical difficulty) is the main hazard on the upper approach — carrying a GPS track or recent trip-report beta is strongly recommended. In early October the creek is crossed on logs, one of which was rotting at its far end.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — essentially every accessible way off Gunn's summit block funnels back through the same notch, ledge, and ramp used going up, so this is fundamentally a downclimb/walk-off rather than a rappel route, with one optional short rappel commonly used at the crux. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3 blocks back to the notch between the peak's two summit 'horns,' then reverse the narrow, roughly one-foot-wide dirt/heather ledge traversing the north face — this exposed traverse is the route's crux in both directions and is meaningfully more dangerous descending when wet, icy, or snow-covered; less experienced parties should consider a handline here. Below the ledge, downclimb back through the class 3-4 notch move to the 'hidden ramp,' a roughly 10-ft, near-vertical step in the cliff band with two options: a chockstone-choked gully (near class 5) on the left, or a more exposed class 3-4 line to the right. This ramp is the one spot on the peak where parties commonly rappel instead of downclimbing — parties describe a sling/rappel station left on a horn or chockstone here (a natural anchor, not bolted; inspect and back it up before trusting it), and a single rappel of roughly 15-20 m clears the step, so a 30 m rope doubled is more than sufficient. Confident scramblers frequently downclimb this section unroped instead, and some parties opt to rappel the steeper gully just right of the ramp when it is wet, icy, or holding snow rather than the ramp itself. Below the ramp, re-cross the talus basin, regain the boot path, and climb back up to the ridge crest (~5,400 ft) before dropping down the switchbacking forest trail, re-crossing Barclay Creek at the log jam, and following the old spur road back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.
hazards: steep brush (alder, devil's club, salmonberry) on the lower approach
loose rock
narrow, ~1-ft-wide exposed ledge/ramp on the summit block, dangerous when wet
route-finding — the climbers' path is unmaintained and easy to lose, especially in the old clear-cut and boulder field
log-jam creek crossing of Barclay Creek can be slick

waysIn.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
waysIn.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
waysIn.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak

waysIn.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
waysIn.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
waysIn.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow and avalanche danger has been judged low; once it melts out, the summer line is the right choice.

name: Gunnshy Peak Standard Route (Barclay Lake Approach)
approach: From Monroe, drive east on US-2 to the town of Baring. Near milepost 41-42, across from a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE. Cross the railroad tracks and continue about 0.3 mile to a junction; keep left on 635th Place NE for another 0.1 mile, where the road becomes Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road). Continue roughly 3.9-4.3 miles of gravel forest road (watch for potholes and rough patches; AWD/4x4 recommended after wet weather) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead (vault toilet on site, parking for roughly 20 vehicles, Northwest Forest Pass required). From a spur road near the trailhead, follow the spur toward an old fire pit, where a faint, mostly-unmarked climber's path heads east into the forest and begins the ascent proper. Partway up the steep forested section the path can seem to stop at a gully; the continuing bootpath leaves to the climber's left, and the gully itself goes only at greater difficulty.
descent: There is no separate descent route; parties retrace the ascent. The steep, brushy headwall and the waterfall gully crossing are the two sections most worth downclimbing carefully and in daylight — wet rock in the gully and loose footing on the headwall are the main hazards on the way down. In early season or after fresh snow, the open slopes above the saddle and the bypass around Point 5,760+ can be icy or avalanche-prone; reversing this section requires the same care as the ascent.
hazards: Loose rock and exposed scrambling on the summit block.
A seasonal waterfall/creek crossing with slick rock underfoot, worst in winter/spring high water.
Avalanche-prone, icy terrain in winter and spring.
A steep, brushy, largely unmarked climber's path with significant route-finding difficulty.

waysIn.name: Barclay Lake spur road to the east ridge
waysIn.season: Mid-July to October
waysIn.notes: There is no official trail. From a spur road near the Barclay Lake trailhead a faint climbers' path heads east into the forest and leads most of the way up. Cross Barclay Creek on logs, leave the old roadbed, and take steep zigzags through the southern slope to a headwall around 3,600 ft. The path then veers east beneath cliff bands and makes a short steep drop into a gully where water dribbles off the rock overhead — dry by late summer, a real flow in winter and spring. Above it cairns lead onto moderate ground, then meadows along the east side of Tailgunner's south ridge to a saddle near 5,400 ft.
hazards: Faint, unmarked climbers' path with sustained route-finding
Slick rock in the seasonal waterfall gully
Heavy slide alder and devil's club if you drift north out of the correct line
Loose rock and exposure on the summit block
Icy, avalanche-prone open slopes in winter and spring

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (1,400', on the Suiattle River Road/FR-26 — the road is closed to vehicles at milepost 12, about 8 miles short of the trailhead; while it stays closed, add that road walk or ride to the hike and check its status first), follow Downey Creek Trail #768. The maintained tread climbs gently along Downey Creek, crossing five tributary creeks (one draining Downey/Pilot Lakes can be a difficult ford in spring high water) and passing informal camps at roughly 1.6, 3, 3.5, and 4 miles before reaching the Bachelor Creek crossing at 6.6 miles/2,400'. Expect old-growth blowdown across the tread in places and a brushy avalanche-chute crossing opposite Green Mountain. At Bachelor Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers'/boot path, which follows the north side of the creek (parties report an improved use-trail here that avoids older brushy sections) up to Bachelor Flats and Bachelor Meadows — the common first-night camp and most parties' Day 1 stop. From Bachelor Meadows continue up steepening open slopes to Cub Pass, then drop about 700' to Cub Lake and cross the meadows beyond it to gain Itswoot Ridge/Itswoot Pass. From Itswoot Pass, step onto the Dome Glacier and rope up for crevasse-hazard glacier travel, traversing to the broad Chikamin-Dome col (~8,500'), a well-established, wind-sheltered camp used as a high camp by most parties (over 7,000 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead to this point). From the col, a further descending traverse (roughly 90 minutes) drops onto the Chikamin Glacier to a snow bench/rock outcrop around 7,000-7,500' directly below Gunsight's west face — many parties move camp here or simply day-climb from the col. Route-finding on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path and Cub Pass/Itswoot Ridge sections, plus crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chikamin Glaciers, are the main approach-specific concerns; carry a rope, crevasse rescue gear, and be comfortable with off-trail alpine travel.
descent: Reverse the ridge crest from the summit: belay/downclimb the exposed summit ridge back down to a large horn about 50' below the true summit that is thickly slung with rappel webbing (a good on-route confirmation marker). From there, make a double-rope (60m x 2) rappel down the West Face to regain the base of the route's black basaltic dike/dihedral. Scramble down several hundred feet of Class 3 terrain on the dike to the top of the crux dihedral, then make a second, diagonal double-rope (60m x 2) rappel — the last person down should place a directional piece of protection to keep the rope running true — which in one pull reaches the snow finger below. From the snow finger, downclimb or glissade back onto the Chikamin Glacier and reverse the approach (re-climb to the Chikamin-Dome col, cross the Dome Glacier, over Itswoot Pass/Cub Pass, down Bachelor Meadows/Bachelor Creek, and out Downey Creek Trail #768) to the trailhead. All anchors reported on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, and chockstones — with no fixed/bolted stations, consistent with its remote, low-traffic character. Typical parties use two 60m ropes for both rappels; expect the crux dihedral's black rock to be loose in spots, and factor in real crevasse-travel time and daylight for the long glacier return to camp.
hazards: Gendarmed multi-summit ridge with several named towers - route-finding error prone in cloud/fog
Chikamin Glacier crossing (done twice, to and from the base of the climb) with hairline-to-open crevasses that worsen later in the season
loose rock in the basalt dike and upper gully sections
true summit is a tiny exposed horn (~barstool-sized) - big exposure tagging it, climbers go one at a time
extremely remote - full 2-day approach each way, no cell coverage, self-rescue only

waysIn.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the first col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.
hazards: Crevasses on the Dome and Chikamin Glaciers, with the Chikamin crossing done to and from the base of the climb; hairline to open late season
Descending traverse from the Chikamin-Dome col onto the Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face needs a rope
Loose rock in the basalt dike and upper gully; the dike is softer than the granite around it
Exposed narrow summit ridge, and a barstool-sized summit horn that holds one climber at a time
Gendarmed multi-summit ridge: route-finding errors are easy in cloud or fog
Over 7,000 ft of gain and a multi-day approach from Downey Creek: no cell coverage, self-rescue only
Rappel descent in two double-rope stages; natural anchors only, black dihedral rock loose in spots

waysIn.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek
waysIn.notes: Take the boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then hike south on the Pacific Crest Trail up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek on logs and scramble northwest to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Creek pass, then cross onto the Chickamin Glacier for the standard line. Expect a long off-trail day with real bushwhacking.
hazards: Long boat-and-shuttle approach: Stehekin boat, then a road shuttle to High Bridge, so a fixed schedule on both ends
About ten miles up Agnes Creek on the Pacific Crest Trail, then off-trail with real bushwhacking to Spruce Creek
Log crossings of Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek
Crevasse hazard on the Chickamin Glacier; rope up moving to and from the glacier bench camp below the west face
Glacier bench camp is cold and fully exposed; site the tent clear of the fall line off the face
Loose rock in the basalt dike and an exposed summit ridge with a one-at-a-time summit horn
Extremely remote: no cell coverage, self-rescue only
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the Stehekin side; the ferry and shuttle logistics are the cost, then a steep off-trail climb from Spruce Creek to a high camp, instead of the Downey Creek route.

name: Improbable Traverse
approach: From Alpental Ski Area parking lot (3,120 ft), reach the talus cone below the west face by a line that stays off the private Alpental Community Club roads; the 'Strasse' roads off the access road are closed to walking and driving, and no established path exists. Approach time ~30 minutes to 1 hour from parking. In early August a public roadside pullout just past the private Strasse entrance serves as parking; keep to the left side of the talus where the rock is less loose.
descent: After summiting via Improbable Traverse, most climbers traverse north over Guye's north and middle summits to descend via established gully systems. A climbers' trail descends from the Guye-Snoqualmie saddle area. For faster/safer descent, fixed anchors (tree with rap tatters) provide rappel opportunity on east side of summit to bypass exposure. Southeast Couloir descent toward Cave Ridge parking is viable alternative.
hazards: High objective rockfall danger: November 2021 rockfall event destroyed major section of route with 30x40ft section falling off
Traverse pitch now requires 5.9-5.10 downclimbing ~20 feet from old piton with 30+ feet of additional unprotected climbing
Very loose and crumbly rhyolite rock throughout route; poor rock quality except for traversing ledges
Intense afternoon sun exposure on west-facing wall intensifies rockfall danger and afternoon weather deterioration
Avalanche blasting from nearby Mount Snoqualmie ski resort in winter (contact 425-434-7669 for alerts)

waysIn.name: Talus cone below the west face
waysIn.season: Jun-Oct
waysIn.notes:
Same problem and same ground as the rest of the west face. The roads named 'Strasse' off the Alpental access road are private; since 2021 the Alpental Community Club has forbidden both driving and walking on them, and climbers have been confronted by residents. The talus field has to be reached by a line that avoids private land, and no established path exists.

The route begins at the top of the talus cone below the face. Reckon on roughly half an hour to an hour from wherever you park to the top of the cone, and wear a helmet on the talus.
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the historic approach crosses private roads residents forbid
loose mossy slab scrambled unroped above the talus
a snow cone at the base of the slabs in early season
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus cone
poor rock quality on all but the traverse pitch

name: North Route ("Hidden Ridge" variation)
approach: The documented north-side line to Guye Peak leaves from the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,080-3,120 ft) via the separate, unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain boot path, which splits off about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail sign — this is a different trailhead path than the West Face/Improbable Traverse talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak (roughly 1.5 miles, reported around 4,500-4,600 ft). From the saddle, turn right (south) and follow the ridge toward Guye's north summit; the standard line follows a steep gully system rated class 3 in summer. Climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and gully sections, so a helmet is worth wearing once off-trail. A short 'Hidden Ridge' variation near the north summit traverses right to an outcropping where a horn can be slung for a single ~30 ft rappel into the north/middle notch, adding one 5.4 move of class 4/low-5th climbing.
descent: The North Route tops out on the same summit ridge system as Guye's other routes, so the descent is the standard south-to-north traverse/rappel sequence rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the summit reached, scramble/downclimb toward the notch between the middle and north summits, where fixed rappel rings are already slung/bolted into the rock — enough parties found the step steep enough to rig it permanently that a rope-assisted descent (roughly 30-40 ft, single strand or doubled off a shorter rope) is the norm rather than the exception. If your line tops out further south, you'll first need to negotiate the notch between the south and middle summits, which is loose mossy class 3/4 slab commonly rappelled off tree-sling anchors (30-60 ft). A related variation sometimes climbed on this side of the peak, the 'Hidden Ridge' line, itself uses a short 30-40 ft rappel mid-route (leaving the rope in place and top-roping back up), which can add confusion about anchor locations if you're relying on other parties' beta — the rap rings at the middle/north notch are the ones relevant to a normal summit-to-car descent. From the north summit, follow the well-defined scrambler's trail down past a small pond, then swing west back to the Alpental lot. Carry a single 30m+ rope, rap device, and a prussik/cordelette to back up any weathered slings; expect climber-triggered rockfall risk in the gullies, worse when snow patches remain into early summer (the steep gullies here can hold snow into a normal season and feel considerably more serious with snow in them than the bare-rock class 3 of summer conditions).
hazards: mossy, dirty class 3/4 slabs on the traverse between the north and middle/south summits
steep connecting gullies between the three summits that fill with snow and become avalanche-prone in winter/spring — check the NWAC forecast before early-season attempts
loose rock typical of the peak generally

waysIn.name: Cave Ridge saddle from Alpental
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct; also done as a winter scramble with axe and traction
waysIn.notes:
From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead area (about 3,080-3,120 ft), take the unmarked climbers' boot path that leaves the pavement close to the Snow Lake trail sign — the one that serves Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, not the west-face talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, roughly a mile and a half in and reported around 4,500-4,600 ft.

From the saddle, turn right (south) and work toward Guye's north summit. Helmets are worth wearing from the point you leave the trail; climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and in the gully.

This peak is also reached from the northbound PCT trailhead through Commonwealth Basin, which is the east side of the mountain — a different approach to a different aspect.
hazards: moat against a large rock face around 4,840 ft if you take the right-hand line
steep snow traverse on the left-hand bypass
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus and in the gully
very steep gully - class 3 in summer, considerably more serious under snow

name: North Slopes via Blum Lakes
approach: Park at the Baker River trailhead at the end of the Baker Lake road (about 800 ft). Walk the Baker River trail for a few minutes to the Blum Creek bridge, then take the faint, flagged climbers' path up the north side of Blum Creek. It is brushy at first, then steep forest to about 4,500 ft; traverse up and south to a talus field near 4,900 ft and cross to Lower Blum Lake, then follow the path to Upper Blum Lake (about 5,020 ft). Travel off the path is very difficult (devil's club, blueberry, brush). North Cascades National Park rules apply: a backcountry permit and camping limits.
descent: Reverse the route. The descent takes as long as the ascent; the path below the lakes is easy to lose, and the Blum Creek crossing gets harder once the snow bridge melts.
hazards: Crevasses and a moat on the Hagan Glacier
Steep snow and cornices on the ridge in spring and early summer
Exposed Class 3-4 rock on the summit block
Dense brush and an easily lost path below the lakes

name: South Slopes
approach: This is the southern way onto Hagan, used mostly by parties on a longer traverse with Bacon Peak and Mount Blum; for the peak alone, the usual line is the North Slopes route by the Blum Lakes. Park at the Baker River Trailhead, the end of FR 11 (Baker Lake Highway), elevation roughly 800 ft. Start on Baker River Trail #606, which follows the true-right bank of the Baker River upstream through mossy old-growth forest — mostly flat, easy tread. At about 0.6 mile the trail crosses the river on a suspension bridge. Shortly after, a rerouted section drops steeply down a bank to ford a side creek and climbs back out through deadfall; this crossing gets wet and can be genuinely difficult or impassable during high runoff (spring snowmelt or after heavy rain) — plan around low-water conditions. The trail then enters North Cascades National Park and continues roughly another mile to Sulphide Creek Camp near the Sulphide Creek/Baker River confluence, about 2.6 miles and only ~170 ft of gain from the trailhead — this is the last maintained tread, the last reliable easy water, and a common bivy for a two-day trip. From near Sulphide Creek Camp, leave the trail and begin a steep, unmarked, use-path-at-best bushwhack climbing north/northeast up the valley wall through old growth and brush toward a small unnamed tarn at roughly 4550-4600 ft informally called 'Hidden Lake' (not the maintained, signed Hidden Lake Trail #745 near Marblemount, which is a different area entirely) — this gains close to 3,700 ft in a little over a mile with no tread. From the tarn, continue bushwhacking north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands that form the route-finding crux of the approach; parties pick brushy ramps and weaknesses to keep the grade climbable. Above the cliffbands the forest breaks into open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank around 6000-6400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. From the benches, ascend a broad talus-and-scree couloir to the southwest end of the Hagan Mountain crags, then make a rising, crevasse/moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier (rope and crampons recommended even in summer) to reach the col between Hagan's twin summits, finishing with a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs to the summit (listed 7067-7080 ft). Overall this is one of the more sustained, taxing approaches in the North Cascades — heavy old-growth/slide-alder bushwhacking, two cliffband route-finding sections, loose scree, and a glacier crossing — which is why it is very commonly combined with Mount Blum (and sometimes Bacon Peak) into a multi-day traverse rather than done as a single out-and-back day.
descent: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb, reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the slabs back to the col/notch between Hagan's twin summits, re-cross the moat, and retrace the rising traverse around the Hagan Glacier's ice apron (rope up again if you did on the way in — moat and crevasse hazard is the same in both directions). Continue down the broad scree/talus couloir to the heather benches on the south flank, then descend back through the two cliffbands — this is the trickiest part to reverse cleanly since the weaknesses threaded on the way up are easy to lose from above; take note of your ascent line (photos, cairns, or a GPS track) before committing. From below the cliffbands, continue the steep bushwhack descent past the small tarn ('Hidden Lake') back down to the Baker River valley floor, rejoin Baker River Trail #606 near Sulphide Creek Camp, and hike the remaining ~2.6 miles out to the trailhead. Parties who combine Hagan with Mount Blum or a longer Blum-Hagan-Bacon traverse typically continue over connecting ridges/cols instead of reversing this line, but for a standalone South Slopes ascent, downclimbing the ascent route is the standard descent. Because of the loose rock in the couloir and the brushy, unmarked cliffband sections, the descent is commonly reported as slower and more error-prone than the climb — budget extra daylight.
hazards: routefinding among Hagan's several summits
afternoon thunderstorms
steep, trail-less bushwhacking through two forest cliff bands on the approach
loose rock in the summit scree/talus couloir
biting insects (blackflies, mosquitoes) in mid-summer
crevasse and moat hazard on the short Hagan Glacier crossing below the twin-summit col

waysIn.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
hazards: Steep, trail-less forest with two cliffbands and no marked line; the weaknesses are hard to spot from above on the way down
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir to the col: helmets and a tight party
Crevasse and moat hazard on the Hagan Glacier ice apron, even in summer; rope and crampons
Snow into midsummer and steep heather around the Hidden Lake tarn camp
Several summits on one massif: route-finding errors and wrong-col mistakes are easy
Afternoon thunderstorms
Remote, trail-less ground far from help
waysIn.whyThisWay: When arriving on the Watson, Blum and Bacon traverse, since that party is already on the Bacon side and reaches the saddle from there instead of dropping back to the Blum Lakes basin.

waysIn.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard from lower Blum Lake to the 6,831 ft pass; the rope goes on before the traverse
The Blum climbers' path off the Baker River Trail is faint and brushy, marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif: easy to commit to the wrong gap or summit
Loose scree and talus on the south-side slabs and couloir
Afternoon thunderstorms
Remote, trail-less ground far from help

name: North Ridge
approach: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path toward Kangaroo Pass. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek itself is the common route-finding mistake. Beyond the first mile the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs, so route-finding is tricky in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, a hazard in early season or after new snow. About two miles from the car, cross the last soggy meadow before the path climbs toward Kangaroo Pass and leave it: look up and left (east) for the prominent talus and scree gully that angles back to the deep notch just north of Half Moon. Climb it — a loose slog at the end — to the notch, where the route starts. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek low on the approach; carry what you need above it.
descent: Descend the route. From the summit, downclimb the easy but exposed top of the ridge to the first anchor and rappel back down the line of ascent, using the ledges on the crest and its west side as stations, until you are back in the notch north of the peak. Carry two ropes; the stations are a mix of old fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts, some parties have found no fixed anchors at all, and any tat left there should be inspected and backed up. From the notch, descend the loose scree gully carefully (keep the party close to limit rockfall), and at its foot rejoin the climbers' path and follow it back north to the hairpin pullout on the highway. In mid-September the top pitch was descended on a single-rope rappel, and from the lower ledges a hidden anchor (a nut plus a horn) lies a scramble away, first climber's left then right; the last rappel from the first-pitch ledge drops straight to the ground with no need to traverse.
hazards: Friable, hollow rock on the first pitch or two; test holds and protect carefully until the rock improves
Lingering snow in the approach gully and the shaded notch north of Half Moon into early-mid July
Loose scree in the gully up to the notch; rockfall onto anyone below
Rappel anchors are old, sparse or missing in some years; carry cord to rebuild them
Exposed traverse on the west side of the upper ridge

waysIn.name: Hairpin pullout and the scree gully to the notch north of Half Moon
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Park at the large pullout on the hairpin near milepost 163 and take the unsigned climbers' path south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek is the standard error here. Beyond the first mile the path crosses boulder fields and slab benches with occasional cairns and all but disappears on the slabs. About two miles from the car, before the path climbs to Kangaroo Pass, cross the last soggy meadow and look left: a talus and scree gully angles back to the deep notch immediately north of Half Moon, and the North Ridge starts in that notch.
hazards: The avalanche path shedding off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak
Loose scree and rockfall in the gully to the notch with any party above
Cairns and tread vanish on the slab benches in fog or fresh snow
No water above the lower approach

name: Helmet Butte Standard Route
approach: From Coles Corner on US-2 (about 20 miles east of Stevens Pass), take WA-207 north 4.4 miles, turn right onto Chiwawa Loop Road for 1.3 miles, then left onto Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) and follow it roughly 23 miles to its end at the Trinity / Buck Creek Pass Trailhead (about 2,772-2,800 ft). Important: storm damage has closed FR 6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground, cutting off drive-in access to Trinity, and wildfire closures have also shut the road and the Buck Creek Trail - confirm current status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before relying on this approach. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 (signed Buck Creek Pass Trail #789 on Forest Service pages), climbing steadily through forest and along Buck Creek roughly 8.8 miles to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off-trail to the right toward Pass No Pass.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the short Class 3 block on its south side, descend the grassy slopes back through the Pass No Pass notch (or, if the west-side variant was used, back down the steep grass/heather to Buck Creek Pass), rejoin the maintained Buck Creek Pass Trail at about 5,600 ft, and follow it roughly 8.8 miles back down to the Trinity Trailhead.
hazards: Loose rock is present on portions of the otherwise solid granodiorite/quartz diorite summit block
Off-trail travel above 5,600-5,800 ft requires route-finding through braided boot paths
Steep grass/heather slopes on the west-side variant lose traction badly when wet
The approach is long and remote (~17.6 miles round trip) with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Buck Creek Trail to Pass No Pass
waysIn.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the high meadows melt out. The alternative grass-and-heather line is likely hazardous when wet.
waysIn.notes: From the highway junction take the state route north, then the loop road and the Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) to its end at the Trinity trailhead. Check current road status before committing to the drive: the road has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, which cuts off drive-in access entirely. From the trailhead hike the Buck Creek trail, climbing steadily through forest and along the creek to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off to the right. This is normally done as part of a backpacking trip to the pass rather than in a day, and the peak sits about half a mile northeast of that pass on the crest.
hazards: A false trail lies just before the real cutoff, and on the way down the fork that crosses the creek into the woods is the wrong one
Road access to the trailhead has been closed below it at times, and fire closures have shut the trail — confirm before driving in
The boot path braids into several strands above about 5,800 ft
Exposed meadow crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
A short scramble on the block itself, easy rock but genuinely a scramble

waysIn.name: Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes
waysIn.season: Midsummer into early autumn on dry ground only — this line is likely hazardous when the grass and heather are wet.
waysIn.notes: The alternative stays on the trail past the off-trail turn and continues all the way to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes from the pass to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble to the top. It is the option for a party already camped at the pass on a backpacking trip, and it trades the braided boot path and the meadow traverse for a steeper direct climb.
hazards: Steep grass and heather with poor runout, and likely hazardous when wet
No path on the climb from the pass
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
The same short scramble on the block itself
Exposed to afternoon weather with no shelter
waysIn.whyThisWay: When already camped at Buck Creek Pass on a backpacking trip, trading the break-off boot path for a steeper direct climb; only on dry ground, as wet grass and heather turn dangerous.

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Goodell Creek Campground/Trailhead on SR 20 just west of Newhalem (~600 ft), follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. This grassy/gravel roadbed is flat and easy hiking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn/stone marker (climbers call it the 'stone arrow') at the end of the roadbed - this marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. This user trail is steep, root-and-duff footing, and brushy in spots (slide alder, devil's club low down) but stays reasonably distinct with flagging/cairns in the upper sections; there is no reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block - a scenic, easier-angle respite after the timber grind. From Stump Hollow, rising-traverse on meadow, slab, and (early/mid-season) snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. Cross the Barrier itself by one of two options: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt; either takes under an hour but involves loose rock and some exposure, so care with rockfall onto any party below is essential. Descend the far side into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites and reliable running water, roughly below Mt. Terror) - this is the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives. From camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col: in early season this is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top; by late season the gully turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left (climber's) side. From the col, the standard route continues up easier ground (scrambling to low 5th class) onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit. Total approach distance to the summit and back runs on the order of 15-16 miles round trip with substantial elevation gain and loss, so most parties treat this as a 2-4 day trip with a basecamp in Crescent Creek Basin rather than a car-to-car push.
descent: Descend by reversing the route: downclimb (with short rappels where the rock steepens or is wet/icy) from the summit back down to the Himmel-Otto col, then retrace the approach gully back down into Crescent Creek Basin. Early in the season this gully descent is a quick, straightforward snow glissade/plunge-step with minimal fuss; by late season, when the gully has melted out to icy hardpack and choss-filled moats, parties often find fixed or placed rap anchors in the moat sections more reliable than downclimbing loose rock next to hard snow/ice. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the entire approach: recross the Barrier (lower ledge or upper moat/choss option), drop back through Stump Hollow, and pick up the steep climbers' path back down through the timber to the old Goodell Creek roadbed and out to the trailhead. There are no bolted or fixed rappel stations on this route - any anchors encountered or built (slings around horns/blocks/chockstones) are natural, climber-placed gear anchors typical of this remote, seldom-visited range, so carry a small rack of slings/cord and a couple of rappel-rated tat-worthy items in case the moat or upper gully requires a rappel to protect the loose, exposed terrain near the col. A single 60m rope is adequate for any rappels on this route (the terrain near the col is broken into short steps, not a sustained wall). Watch for rockfall in the gully and on the Barrier crossings, especially with parties above, and for the choss/loose-rock hazard around the overhanging boulder bypass near the col, which is exposed in both directions.
hazards: sustained exposure
loose/chossy rock on the upper peak and approach gully
remoteness — a full-day approach each way with no quick escape
The Barrier crossing between Terror and Crescent Creek basins: steep, loose, exposed traverse
route-finding through brush and cliff bands on the Goodell Creek approach
lingering moats and icy snow in the Himmel-Otto col gully in early/late season

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct
waysIn.notes: From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives.
hazards: An icy, choss-and-moat gully to the col in late season
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass
Two Barrier crossings, both loose and exposed, with rockfall onto any party below
No reliable water between the Goodell roadbed and treeline
No bolted or fixed rappel stations anywhere on the route; all anchors are built

name: Wild Hair Crack
approach: Via Goodell Creek Trailhead (~600 ft) and the Stump Hollow approach into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites below Mt. Terror), then a narrow gully up to the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col.
descent: Early in the season, straightforward reverse scrambling suffices. Later in the season, rappel anchors found in the moats are helpful; a single 60m rope is workable with planning, though double ropes give more flexibility. An alternative is a series of rappels and exposed scrambling down the NW side back toward the col.
hazards: Late-season moats can be icy and choked with loose choss, sometimes requiring an overhanging-boulder bypass.
The Southern Pickets basin is remote enough that a nearby 2009 accident on Mt. Terror required a multi-day rescue.

name: Honeymoon Route
approach: From the Upper Dungeness/Royal Basin Trailhead (elev. ~2,500 ft), hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about a mile farther into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), a meadow-and-tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba, and Hal Foss Peak. From the upper basin, leave the trail and head southwest over the moraine to the big snow slope on the west edge of the northeast face. Climb it most of the way toward the low point of the Deception-Martin ridge, then break left into the steep side gully that gives the route its name; from its top, traverse left and climb a second snow-and-rock gully to the summit ridge. Allow roughly 3 hours from the upper basin to the top of the gully in good snow. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead and a wilderness permit is required for overnight stays. In early May water runs freely beside the trail up to roughly 5,700 ft, so there is no need to melt snow on the way in.
descent: Climbers typically downclimb or glissade the couloir if snow conditions allow, or traverse to descend via the standard route's looser terrain; either way the exit funnels back through upper Royal Basin to Royal Lake and the maintained trail.
hazards: Pillow-lava rock makes rockfall 'inevitable' on this route, with a history of serious injuries and fatalities.
Recent documented incident (May 2026): a climber took a 300 ft fall and required a helicopter rescue.

Route-finding is inconsistent and sparsely cairned; parties have strayed from the standard gully into steeper terrain north of the saddle, encountering unexpected class 4 climbing and 20-ft cliff bands.
The Royal Basin approach includes an unbridged, ill-defined stream crossing between Royal Lake and the upper basin.

Persistent low cloud and fast-moving weather fronts frequently obscure the route itself — the peak's name derives from historical difficulty locating a line through cloud cover, and modern parties report the same issue.

waysIn.name: Royal Basin to the Northeast Couloir
waysIn.season: Apr-Jun, while the gully still holds snow
waysIn.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness / Royal Basin Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail and then the Royal Basin Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about another mile into Upper Royal Basin at roughly 5,600 ft — a meadow and tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba and Hal Foss.

A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead, and Royal Lake is an Olympic National Park quota area, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the upper basin, leave the trail and cross the moraine southwest to the snow slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, where the climb begins. Allow about three hours from the upper basin to the top of the gully.
hazards: loose rotten rock throughout the upper mountain
snow in the gully in early season, and the left-branching variation melts out by late season
scree and talus in the basin
steep and exposed ground on a peak generally described as serious

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Libby Lake Trailhead (a.k.a. Libby Creek Trailhead, ~4,430 ft; no parking fee or pass required at this trailhead) at the end of Libby Creek Road, follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs gradually through mixed conifer forest and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks (trekking poles help); tread can be brushy/overgrown in the lower stretches. The first reliable water is a spring in the burn scar, and the ford of North Fork Libby Creek, about halfway to Libby Lake, has a campsite on the far bank. At about 4.5 miles you reach a decaying historic line cabin in a clearing — the key junction on this route: continuing straight/west climbs a final steep half-mile (~470 ft) to Libby Lake (7,740 ft), a common basecamp and especially scenic in larch season (late Sept–early Oct), while the right-hand fork is the climbers' route toward Hoodoo. The route does not go to Libby Lake: take the faint boot path to the right of the cabin into open forest, then pick a line up the boulder field and loose gully to the pass on the ridge south of the summit. Once off-trail there is no maintained tread and the boulder field has no single obvious line, so route-finding care is needed — this is the route's main hazard, especially in fog or flat light. From the ridge crest, turn north and follow it over a broad boulder field to the summit; the final stretch is continuous class 2 boulder-hopping with occasional class 3 moves, and loose rock is common, so test holds before weighting them. Snow can linger in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June, so carry an ice axe (crampons recommended) for May–June attempts.
descent: The standard descent is a straight reversal of the ascent: back down the summit boulder field to the pass south of the summit, down the entry gully and boulder field to the old cabin, and out Libby Creek Trail No. 415 to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/scramble descent with no rappelling required (rappels: 0) — no ropes, anchors, or technical gear are needed on the standard route. Some parties descend slightly skier's-left (east) of their ascent line through looser scree for a more direct, faster line off the boulder field, but this variation is steeper and looser underfoot, so it's a judgment call rather than the default. The main descent hazard is footing in the unstable talus/boulder field rather than exposure — most reported close calls on Hoodoo come from rolled ankles or shifting rock, not falls. Note that a connecting ridge traverse to neighboring Raven Ridge is a distinct, harder outing involving an exposed knife-edged 4th-class section and at least one short technical rappel/downclimb near a rock overhang — that beta belongs to the traverse route, not to this standard scramble.
hazards: Loose talus and rockfall in the boulder slopes and gully leading to the ridge/pass — helmet recommended and stay alert for parties below
Unmarked, unmaintained route above the old cabin near the Libby Lake trail junction — easy to lose the line in the boulder field, especially in poor visibility
Sudden weather changes — multiple trip reports (including early October) describe snow flurries and wind on the ridge/summit despite clear starts
Lower trail passes through the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire burn zone; burned-out roots have left hidden holes underfoot
Long approach and long day (car-to-car reports range roughly 6.5–9.5 hrs) with no water above Libby Lake

waysIn.name: Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake
waysIn.season: July into early October; especially popular in late September and early October when the basin and approach slopes fill with golden larch. Snow can hold in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the wilderness. The tread climbs gradually through mixed conifer and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks, and can be brushy and overgrown low down. A spring in the patchwork burn scar and then the ford of the North Fork of Libby Creek are the reliable water, with an established campsite on the far bank. At roughly four and a half miles a decaying old cabin stands in the middle of the trail, and that is where the climbing route leaves. Note that the standard line does not go to Libby Lake at all — the lake is the left-hand continuation and a fine camp, but the peak is reached from the cabin.
hazards: Brushy, lightly maintained tread and unbridged tributary crossings low down
The boot path fades in the clearing above the cabin and there are no cairns anywhere on the route
Choose-your-own-line boulder hopping to gain the ridge, with harder and easier ways and no defined route
Loose and unstable blocks on the summit ridge; test holds before weighting them
Lingering snow into June
Downloadable tracks for this peak are known to be wrong — do not follow one blindly

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of the Cascade River Road — gravel/washboard, high-clearance/AWD recommended), climb the well-graded Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks 3.7 mi and about 1,800 ft to the broad 5,400-ft saddle at Cascade Pass. Two standard lines converge on Horseshoe Peak from here, both eventually crossing loose, unmaintained terrain above the pass. Sahale Arm option: continue past the Cascade Pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail, climbing the open heather ridge past the Doubtful Lake overlook to Sahale Glacier Camp (about 5.9 mi and 3,940 ft of gain from the trailhead, ~7,600 ft). From camp, traverse east across the boulder/heather plateau below Sahale Glacier (passing roughly a dozen established camp pads), downclimb a steep snowfield (whippet or axe useful, can be firm/icy into midsummer), then traverse east to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge. Follow a cairned climber's trail down the ridge, negotiating one short 4th-class step, into a scree/talus gully that drops to a snowfield around 6,600 ft. Cross this snowfield into Horseshoe Basin, traverse a wide ledge at ~6,600 ft rising gradually to ~6,800 ft at the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine, then continue on loose scree/talus contouring to a stance south/southeast of Horseshoe Peak below the crest of Ripsaw Ridge. Lower Horseshoe Basin option (more direct, more elevation loss/regain): from Cascade Pass, drop east into Pelton Basin (established camp; reliable water at Doubtful Creek/Pelton Basin — fill up here, since Horseshoe Basin's own water is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk) and work cross-country toward the Black Warrior mine gully, a narrow (~8-ft-wide) rock dike dropping about 100 ft to the Horseshoe Basin side: Class 3 at the top, a short Class 4 downward step to an alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it, then continuing Class 3 but loose and exposed. From the basin floor (~6,600 ft) contour northeast then east on slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge below the summit notch. Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself, so most parties base at Sahale Glacier Camp or Pelton Basin and day-trip the peak from there — for a round trip of about 14 miles (22.5 km). Either way, expect extended travel on loose talus/scree and slabs with real fall exposure, a snow crossing that wants an axe (crampons in early season), and route-finding by cairn/climber's trail rather than maintained tread once past Sahale Arm or Pelton Basin.
descent: Reverse the approach. From the base of the gully/ledge leading to Horseshoe's summit, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 to a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the true summit, exiting on a loose Class 3/4 ledge to the highpoint — a small, roughly one-meter-square notch atop Ripsaw Ridge. There is a solid rock horn on the east side of the notch that serves as the natural rappel anchor (parties also build a small gear anchor from a few cams if a horn sling is absent or worn). One rappel of roughly 100 ft (about 30 m) down the south-face ledge system returns you to the notch/gully below the summit: a 30 m rope reaches close to the bottom, with maybe the last 10 ft needing an easy downclimb, while a 60 m rope (doubled) or a single-strand 60 m lower reaches with rope to spare for a clean single rappel. There is no fixed/bolted hardware here — it's a natural horn and/or gear anchor, so carry a few cams as backup. From the base of the rappel, reverse whichever approach line was used: descend the loose gully/ledge back into Horseshoe Basin, re-cross the ~6,600-ft snowfield, and either regain Sahale Peak's ridge and the Sahale Arm Trail back to Cascade Pass, or climb back out of Pelton Basin over Cascade Pass to the trailhead. Loose, exposed rock on the summit ledges is the main descent hazard (helmet recommended, and manage rope carefully to avoid dislodging blocks); the long snow/scree/slab travel back to camp or the trailhead is otherwise straightforward but sustained.
hazards: loose rock / choss throughout the ridge, gully, and dihedral
low prominence saddle traverse
remote position — long, complex approach with no quick bail once in Horseshoe Basin
exposed, unroped Class 3/4 sections above significant drops
fall-would-be-fatal exposure at the short 5.2 summit-notch crux
early-season snow and possible crevasse hazard on Sahale Arm / the Sahale Glacier bowl

waysIn.name: Sahale Arm, the secret gully, and the mining-equipment alcove
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From Sahale Glacier Camp traverse the boulder-and-heather plateau east, downclimb the steep snowfield, and gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge; follow a cairned climbers' trail down it, past one short 4th-class step, descending easterly to about 7,100 ft. Pick up the southeast rib that forms the west edge of Horseshoe Basin and follow it southeast to the top of the so-called secret gully at about 6,700 ft — full of snow some years, completely melted out and loose in others. Below it, traverse a wide ledge at 6,600 ft rising gradually to the base of a cliff at 6,800 ft where old mining workings sit, then contour loose scree until you are due south of the peak. Fill up at Doubtful Creek or Pelton Basin: the water in Horseshoe Basin is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk.
hazards: Extended travel on loose talus, scree and slabs with real fall exposure
A snow crossing that wants an axe, and crampons in early season
Mine-tailings contamination of Horseshoe Basin water
Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself

name: Hourglass Gully (Winter)
approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead and follow Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then traverse talus and boulders around the west side of the lake to its south end. From there head east to a saddle and climb the ridge/gully system southwest of it toward Main Peak, the massif's highest and most technical summit (~5,991 ft). Expect over 6,000 ft of total elevation gain, dense brush and small cliffs on the ridge above the lake, and steep snow in the gully higher up; most parties plan for a 15+ hour car-to-car day or an overnight.
