descent: The descent mirrors the ascent route but is significantly more technical. On the upper East Ridge, climbers set up two 30-meter rappels using existing rap slings in trees. Descending the Hourglass Gully in spring conditions often involves boot-skiing down 40-50 degree slopes with small wet slides. The steep constriction requires careful down-climbing or short rappels. The ridge traverse back to the lake saddle is exposed with 1,000-foot drops to the northeast side. Return to Lake Serene via the approach slope and descend the 4.1-mile trail by headlamp if a very early start was not made.
hazards: Active avalanche paths dominate the Hourglass Gully; the gully is a natural funnel for snow and debris from the upper peak
Icefall and rockfall on the right side of the Hourglass Gully are frequent; this section is the objective hazard pinch-point
Exposure on the upper East Ridge is extreme; a slip or rope failure is likely fatal; this is a serious mountaineering undertaking
Dense brush on the ridge between the lake saddle and the summit is a major objective hazard in summer; winter and spring ascents avoid this via snow
Cornices form on the summit ridge; avoid stepping on cornice edges, especially on the north side

waysIn.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
waysIn.season: Snow cover — roughly late winter through May; not recommended once melted out
waysIn.notes:
Lake Serene trailhead off Mount Index Road at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft to the north end of the lake, where the trail ends.

Traverse the west side of the lake over talus and huge boulders to the south end. In snow, stay lower, closer to the water — the slope is less steep near the shore. Expect massive avalanche debris on this stretch.

From the south end of the lake head east to the saddle, then take the ridge running southwest from it. That forested ridge is the crux of the approach and the reason this is a spring route: roughly the next 1,000 ft is dense brush and intermittent cliffs, plus one airy ten-foot rock step usually climbed by grabbing roots. Snow cover makes the ridge dramatically easier; bare, it is a fight. Plan on 12+ hours car to car and over 6,000 ft of gain despite the peak being under 6,000 ft.
hazards: Steep dense brush and intermittent cliffs on the forested southwest ridge
The airy ten-foot rock step on the ridge, usually climbed on roots
Avalanche debris and avalanche hazard around the lake and in the gully
The wet rock step in the constriction once the gully melts out
Very long day — 12 to 15 hours is normal

name: North Route (North Peak)
approach: The border gate at Hozomeen has been closed to vehicles and walkers until further notice, so Silver-Skagit Road from Hope, B.C. no longer reaches the trailhead; from the US side Hozomeen is reached by boat up Ross Lake or on the 31-mile East Bank Trail from SR 20. Start at the Hozomeen ranger station, elevation about 1,600 ft, and follow the little Trail of the Obelisk loop. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on Hozomeen's western flank. There is no trail from here on; the forest is passable on the ascent but reports describe dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as a serious time sink on the way down. Continue to a heathery knoll at about 5,900 ft where you gain the north ridge proper. Round trip is roughly 15 miles with 6,800 ft of gain and the same in loss.
descent: There are no shortcuts off this mountain and no rappels. Downclimb the northeast ridge, taking the exposed 7,600 ft segment with the same care you gave it on the way up - it is worse in soft afternoon conditions. Descend the north cirque snowfields facing in where they are firm, plunge-stepping or glissaging where they are soft, then regain the north ridge and reverse its several bumps. The real toll is the forest below the 5,900 ft knoll: dense brush and jackstraw deadfall on the west flank made the descent slow enough that one party logged 6.0 hours down against 7.1 hours up, an unusually small gap that tells you how much of the time is spent in the trees. Carry a track; the flank has no distinguishing features and reversing your ascent line matters.
hazards: Rockfall from the friable Hozomeen chert on the upper ridge and in the cirque, both natural and party-generated.
Steep snow in the north cirque, firm and fall-prone in the morning, wet and slide-prone by afternoon, with no avalanche forecast product covering this corner of the range.
Navigational hazard in the trackless forested approach - the west flank is featureless enough that parties lose serious time reversing it.
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, an international border between the climber and the road, and only a handful of parties on the summit each year.
Access is fragile - the NPS border gate is closed until further notice and Silver-Skagit Road was closed at km 6 by the Border 2 Fire in July 2026.

waysIn.name: The short loop trail at the ranger station, then the west flank to the heather knoll
waysIn.season: July through September, once the west flank is clear of snow
waysIn.notes:
Start at the ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,600 ft and pick up the short interpretive loop that begins there. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on the mountain's western flank. There is no trail above the loop.

The forest goes reasonably on the way up and badly on the way down: parties consistently report dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as the time sink of the descent rather than of the ascent, so mark your line as you climb rather than trusting to memory.
hazards: no trail above the interpretive loop, and a descent through jackstraw deadfall and brush that is far slower than the ascent
a creek crossing at Howlett Creek
route-finding on a uniform forested flank with no landmarks below the knoll
steep snowfields low on the route in early season
loose class 3 and 4 rock on the ridge above
reaching the ranger station at all depends on a boat or on a closed border gate

name: Northeast Buttress (North Peak)
approach: There is no US road to Hozomeen. From the Trans-Canada Highway (BC Hwy 1) take Exit 168 at Hope, British Columbia, follow Flood-Hope Road onto Silver-Skagit Road, and drive roughly 34 miles / 55 km of gravel south through Skagit Valley Provincial Park to the Skyline II trailhead — about an hour and a quarter. Verify road and border status first: Silver-Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, and NPS has prohibited both vehicle and foot traffic across the boundary at Hozomeen since 2020, with no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026. From Skyline II, climb the trail roughly 8 miles and 4,000 ft to the Hozomeen Ridge junction, then turn south on the Hozomeen Ridge Trail over rolling terrain to a camp near the Monument 74 high point at about 6,345 ft, 10.5 miles in. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below Hozomeen Ridge — there is no running water again until you are south of the border. From camp the climb begins by dropping about 545 ft to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque. A shorter but much nastier alternative starts at the Hozomeen ranger station, follows the short Trail of the Obelisk loop, then bushwhacks east up the overgrown border swath past a swamp and gains about 3,000 ft to a col near 6,300 ft before joining the ridge; it saves miles and costs hours.
descent: Descend exactly the way you came up. Downclimb the summit blocks and the exposed 7,600 ft step facing inward, taking the same line you climbed — do not try to shortcut the ledge system, because the north cirque side is undercut and the alternatives cliff out. Below the rock, downclimb the upper snowfield facing in, then plunge-step and glissade the lower snowfield to the saddle. Cold, firm morning snow that took crampons cleanly will be soft and rotten on the way down; the same slope that felt secure at 07:00 can be a wet-slide problem at 15:00, and late-season moats at the snow-rock margin are a real trap. Regain the ridge to camp, then reverse the Hozomeen Ridge and Skyline II trails. Parties who camped and descended in one push report roughly six hours from summit back to the trailhead.
hazards: Rockfall is the dominant objective hazard - the route climbs loose ramps and a ridge of friable metamorphosed basalt, and parties above you will knock material down.
Steep snow in the north cirque presents both a fall hazard on firm morning snow and a wet-loose avalanche hazard on warm afternoons in June and early July.

There is no avalanche forecast for this corner of the range; NWAC's nearest product is the Mt Baker zone and Avalanche Canada's South Coast Inland region abuts it from the north, so both are extrapolation.
Rescue is genuinely slow. There is no cell coverage, the peak is in Whatcom County but your road access is in British Columbia, and the area sees only a handful of parties a year.
Water scarcity above the forest is a real medical hazard on hot approach days; heat exhaustion is reported on these slopes.

waysIn.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
waysIn.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
waysIn.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
hazards: The boundary crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic; the gravel road has also had a wildfire closure
Long gravel drive with no services, then a 4,000 ft trail climb to the ridge
No running water south of the creeks below the ridge junction; dry camp and heat exhaustion risk on hot days
Losing 545 ft to the saddle from camp, which has to be re-climbed on the way out
Rockfall from friable basalt ramps and ridge; parties above knock material down
Steep snow in the north cirque: firm and a fall hazard in the morning, wet-slide prone on warm afternoons; moats late season
No avalanche forecast for the area, no cell coverage, and slow rescue

waysIn.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
waysIn.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
waysIn.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
hazards: Overgrown, steep, brushy boundary swath with no tread: about 3,000 ft of slow bushwhacking
A swamp low on the line
No water on the upper half
Reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
Rockfall from friable basalt ramps and ridge on the buttress itself
Steep snow in the north cirque: fall hazard on firm morning snow, wet slides when warm; moats late season
No avalanche forecast, no cell coverage, and slow rescue
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the lake and ranger station can be reached by boat or the northern road, and a party accepts hours of steep, overgrown brush to save the miles of the long ridge trail.

name: Southwest Route (South Peak)
approach: From the Hozomeen Lake/Willow Lake trailhead at Hozomeen Campground (roughly 1,650-1,720 ft), a maintained trail runs 1.5 to several miles before climbers leave it near Hozomeen Lake's outlet, cross Hozomeen Creek, and push east through heavy deadfall and devil's club into the peak's west basin. This gains a rib/gully system leading to a high camp or bivy around 4,900-5,000 ft, and on to a saddle reported at roughly 6,800 ft below the final pitches.
descent: Descend the line you climbed. From the summit, reverse the narrow west ridge: the short 5.6 headwall below the top is usually rappelled from the anchor on the platform above it, and the overhang lower on the ridge is rappelled from a fixed bolt. Between those the crest is loose, with scree-covered ledges where a slip is serious, and most of the traverse is on the south side of the ridge. Past the overhang, go back around the rib and the broad loose gully to the access notch and drop to the 6,800 ft saddle. From there, descend the west basin: slabs first, then red scree and heather, then the boulder bottleneck, and finally the west rib and the dry creek bed, where deadfall slows everything. Expect devil's club near Hozomeen Creek before rejoining the Hozomeen Lake trail.
hazards: Loose, crumbly rock with limited protection
serious exposure — one party reports roughly 1,000-ft drops on the upper mountain
heavy deadfall and devil's club in the valley approach
water scarcity above the basin later in the season

waysIn.name: The lake-side trail from the campground, leaving it at the Hozomeen Lake outlet for the west basin
waysIn.season: July through September, once the west basin has melted out
waysIn.notes:
From the campground and trailhead at roughly 1,650 to 1,720 ft, a maintained trail runs toward Hozomeen Lake. Climbers leave it near the lake's outlet, cross Hozomeen Creek, and push east into the peak's west basin through heavy deadfall and devil's club - the brush here is the defining feature of the approach rather than an incidental one. The basin gives onto a rib and gully system that leads to a high camp or bivouac around 4,900 to 5,000 ft, and above that to a saddle reported near 6,800 ft below the final pitches.

Getting to the campground itself is the trip's first problem: either the resort water taxi up the lake, or the long gravel road down from the north side of the boundary, which has been closed to vehicles and walkers alike. Settle that before anything else.
hazards: heavy deadfall and devil's club through the whole lower basin
a creek crossing to enter the basin
loose rock on the rib and gully system
an exposed high bivouac with limited flat ground
reaching the trailhead at all, which depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate

name: West Face
approach: Park at the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52, large lot off SR 906/Alpental Rd; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required). Head north on the Pacific Crest Trail; most parties cut the corner via the Commonwealth Basin/Red Pass climbers' shortcut, which rejoins the PCT and trims about a mile off the standard trail. Climb the well-graded PCT switchbacks up to Kendall Katwalk (roughly 5 miles and 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead) — a dramatic ledge blasted into a cliff face with real exposure in a fall-on-snow scenario early season. Continue north on the PCT past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, skirting the base of Alaska Mountain, to where the trail runs above Joe Lake, about 10 miles from the pass. For the West Route, leave the trail at a flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake and head up a talus slope into the basin below the west face, which is clearly visible from there. Alternatively, take the Gold Creek Trail to Joe Lake and hike upslope to the PCT. Water is reliable at Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, and at Joe Lake below the trail. Hazards on the approach include lingering snow on north-facing benches into July, loose rock in the approach gullies and talus once off-trail, and route-finding in poor visibility. Because of the length, many parties split this into 2-3 days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake.
hazards: loose, shattered andesite and rockfall danger in the summit gully — this west line has fallen out of favor versus the East Ridge for this reason
exposed 5.6 climbing on the west face and the summit block
brushy, sometimes indistinct route-finding through tree bands on the lower approach
residual snow in the gully into July on some years

name: South Ridge
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (about 23 miles of pavement then gravel from Marblemount; the upper gravel section is gated and typically doesn't open until snow clears, often not until late June/July). From the trailhead, follow the well-graded, heavily-used Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — the last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so top off bottles before the switchbacks. At the pass, leave the maintained tread and pick up the climbers' path/boot track heading south-southeast, making a rising traverse across snow or heather on the flanks of Mixup Peak to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft); this stretch is loose, choosy, and crosses several snow patches that can be firm in early morning. Ascend moderate glacier/snow slopes (crevasses can open by late summer — rope up if the party isn't comfortable soloing them) to the notch at Cache Col (6,900 ft). From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about 1 mile over loose rock and heather benches, crossing occasional snowfields, down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water source in the basin (may be partly frozen early season). Car-to-camp is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,300 ft of gain, generally a half-day carrying overnight gear. From camp, the peak itself is climbed as a side trip: head up toward Hurry-up Peak's south/southwest flank, crossing a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft (carry an axe/crampons even mid-summer) before gaining broken granite slabs and the south ridge crest; follow the crest/upper gully system with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling and a couple of exposed but short moves along the summit ridge to the 7,821 ft top — about 1 mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly 1-1.5 hours for a fit party.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. From the summit, reverse the ascent line back down the south ridge/gully system, downclimbing the same Class 2-3 granite terrain and re-crossing the steep snow band near 7,100 ft (plunge-step or glissade if conditions allow, but keep the axe out given the exposure just above), back down to Kool-Aid Lake camp — about 3-3.5 hours round trip from camp is typical for the whole side-trip. From camp, descend by reversing the approach: climb back up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes, traverse back around Mixup Peak's flanks to Cascade Pass, then descend the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. No technical descent hazards beyond the approach terrain itself — main concerns are the steep snow crossing near 7,100 ft (harder and icier in early season or late day when it's refrozen) and losing the boot path on the granite benches between Kool-Aid Lake and the ridge, which has multiple similar-looking gully options.
hazards: loose rock
lingering snow
route-finding
crevasses/snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
icy, steep snow on the Cache Col-to-Kool-Aid Lake descent

waysIn.name: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July and wants an axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free
waysIn.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road — the upper gravel section is gated and often does not open until late June or July — follow the well-graded Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low down, so fill up before the switchbacks.

At the pass leave the maintained tread for the climbers' path heading south-southeast, a rising traverse across snow or heather on Mixup Peak's flanks to the base of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft. Ascend moderate glacier and snow slopes to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft. From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock and heather benches to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water in the basin.

From camp the peak is a side trip: up toward the south flank, across a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft, then broken granite slabs to the ridge. About a mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly an hour to an hour and a half for a fit party.
hazards: Crevasses and snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
Icy, steep snow on the Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake descent, worse refrozen in the early morning or late in the day
A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft that wants an axe and crampons even mid-summer
Loose rock and multiple similar-looking gully lines on the granite benches — the main route-finding crux
Short but exposed moves along the summit ridge

name: Southwest Route / Icy Glacier
approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail #674) at road's end on FS Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road), off SR 542 (Mt. Baker Highway), elevation ~3,100 ft. Hike Trail #674 roughly 4 miles, switchbacking up through forest along Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft), gaining ~2,000 ft. The signed Hannegan Camp (~3.5 mi in) is the last reliable water on the trail — fill up there, as there is no running water past it for the rest of the route. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country south, climbing open heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth Mountain's north side (3rd-class terrain through trees in spots), then rope up and ascend the moderate slopes of the Ruth Glacier — crevasses open up here in late season, especially on the upper mountain — to Ruth Mountain's summit (7,115 ft). Most parties treat this as a 5–6 hour trailhead-to-camp day, camping on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond it. From camp, descend Ruth's south/west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp); there are two common lines down — a steep, loose gully some parties call the 'death gully,' or safer heather slopes and a game trail on climber's left (2nd–3rd class) — down to the Ruth–Icy saddle (~5,700 ft). From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier, rope up again, and climb the glacier's northwest slope gradually southeast, keeping the rock ridge on your left and crevasses on your right, to about 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch (watch for a bergschrund near the top some seasons), to reach a notch/saddle west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From there climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd–3rd class talus and snow up Icy's south side to the base of a light-colored, ~100-ft 4th-class summit gully with solid jugs and ledges; this leads to the northwest summit. Note the true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by additional 3rd/4th class scrambling — many parties only tag the northwest summit, which holds the register. Hazards throughout: crevasses on both the Ruth and Icy Glaciers, occasional rockfall on Icy's south-side scramble terrain, black flies and mosquitoes on the lower trail in summer, and essentially no water source after Hannegan Camp. A few moves in the summit gully feel low-fifth class rather than straightforward 4th class, depending on the exact line chosen.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line. Off the summit gully, parties either downclimb the 4th-class rock (described as casual with solid holds) or rig a single rappel: a 60m rope doubled gives about 30m (100 ft) of rope per side, matching the gully's height, anchored on slings/webbing around a rock horn at the top — this is a natural anchor only (no bolts/fixed chains reported), so inspect and back up existing tat before trusting it. From the base of the gully, downclimb the 2nd–3rd class talus/snow back to the Icy Glacier saddle, re-rope and re-cross the Icy Glacier reversing the ascent line, then traverse back to the Ruth–Icy saddle. From there it's roughly 1,400 ft of regain back up to Ruth Mountain's summit (about 900 ft to the notch camp) — the sting in the tail of this traverse — before descending Ruth's north side and the Ruth Glacier back to Hannegan Pass, and hiking the 4-mile trail out to the trailhead. This is a long day (done in a single push it is typically 15-20 hours car-to-car, with a fast party moving for about 12 of them) with significant elevation loss-then-regain between Icy and Ruth; carry a stove or plan water carefully since there's no reliable source between Hannegan Camp and the trailhead on the way out. Watch for loose rock in the summit gully and standard crevasse/glacier hazards in reverse on both glaciers.
hazards: crevasses
lingering snow
loose rock
remote position

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, over Ruth Mountain, then the Icy Glacier's northwest slope to the west notch
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at road's end on FS Road 32, near 3,100 ft, hike Trail #674 roughly four miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft. Hannegan Camp about 3.5 miles in is the last reliable water on the route — fill up there, because there is nothing running past it.

From the pass go cross-country south up heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth's north side, with some third-class ground through trees, then rope up for the Ruth Glacier to Ruth's summit at 7,115 ft. Most parties treat trailhead-to-camp as a five to six hour day and camp on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond.

From camp, descend Ruth's south and west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp) to the Ruth-Icy saddle near 5,700 ft, taking the heather slopes and game trail on climber's left rather than the steep loose gully. From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier.
hazards: No water source at all after Hannegan Camp
Crevasses on both the Ruth and the Icy Glaciers, and a bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock in the summit gully with the whole party funnelled through it — helmets are standard
The steep loose 'death gully' off Ruth, which is the natural fall line and the wrong option
Roughly 1,400 ft of regain from the Ruth-Icy saddle over Ruth on the way home

name: Indian Mountain Scramble
approach: No maintained trail reaches the summit — Indian Mountain is approached cross-country from the Hannegan Pass/Chilliwack River trail system, the only real access into this part of the park. From the Hannegan Trailhead (3,120 ft, end of FR 32/Ruth Creek Road), follow the Hannegan Pass Trail roughly 4-5.6 mi over 5,050-ft Hannegan Pass, then switchback down into the Chilliwack River valley to the Boundary Camp area (about 5.1 mi in) as you cross into North Cascades National Park. Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, crossing the river via the hand-pulled 2-person cable car (replaced Oct. 2019), to the Brush Creek Trail junction (roughly 11-12 mi from the trailhead). From there take the Brush Creek Trail, which climbs through the 2022 Brush Creek Fire burn toward Whatcom Pass (about 5.1 mi one-way from the Brush Creek junction). Indian Mountain rises immediately above this corridor; parties leave the trail below or near Whatcom Pass and work up open heather/talus slopes and ridgelines to the summit, with sustained, often brushy or loose route-finding required in both directions. One-way distance to the summit runs roughly 16 miles, making this realistically a 3-5 day objective, most often combined with a broader Whatcom Pass/Copper Ridge trip rather than climbed stand-alone.
descent: Reverse the wilderness route back to the trail system.
hazards: deep wilderness isolation — no maintained trail or marked route to the summit; off-trail navigation required
long multi-day approach (about 32 mi round trip) through national park backcountry with no quick bailout
major blowdown on the Chilliwack River Trail between the Brush Creek junction and Indian Creek Camp from 2021-22 wildfire damage
post-fire hazards on Brush Creek Trail: rockfall from unstable burned switchbacks and falling branches/snags
aggressive bear activity reported at Chilliwack-drainage camps (Fireweed, South Fork) — hard-sided food storage required
early-season avalanche terrain on the steep approach slopes above Brush Creek Valley
Chilliwack River crossing via hand-pulled cable car; creek crossings can run high with snowmelt
no cell coverage anywhere on the approach or summit

name: East Peak (Low Fifth Class)
approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (FS Road 9737 end, North Fork Teanaway) and follow the Esmeralda Basin/Lake Ingalls Trail (aka Ingalls Way Trail) north along a rushing creek on an old mining-road grade. At about 0.4 mi a signed junction sends the Longs Pass trail off to the right; stay left/straight for Lake Ingalls. The trail climbs at a moderate, steady grade through Headlight Basin for roughly 3 miles to Ingalls Pass (~6500 ft) and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary — this is the crux navigational/physical checkpoint of the hike-in, gaining close to 2,500-2,800 ft from the trailhead. In early season expect lingering snow and ice on the pass switchbacks; microspikes and an ice axe are worth carrying into July. From Ingalls Pass, drop slightly and traverse boulder-hop terrain into the basin below Lake Ingalls, then climb a large, steep boulder field (hands-and-feet scrambling in spots) to reach Lake Ingalls itself at roughly 4 miles from the trailhead. Lake Ingalls is the last reliable water — filter here before continuing, as there is none higher. From the lake, pick up the climbers' path that skirts the east/right shore and heads up the basin toward the obvious notch between the main Ingalls summit and East Peak; favor the clean granite slabs on climber's left over the loose, chossy central gully, which is the main rockfall/loose-rock hazard on the approach. At approximately 7,000 ft, angle toward the North Peak-East Peak notch, where a chockstone marks the start of the climbing (either climb directly to it or downclimb a short section from the East Ridge start to reach it). Total approach is on the order of 5 miles and ~3,500 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead to the base of the route, consistent with this route's ~16 km round-trip distance figure.
descent: The Southwest Face (East Peak's low-fifth-class line) is short — 2 pitches — and the standard descent is to rappel the route itself: three rappel stations are encountered descending the line, using natural anchors (slings around the chockstone/horns typical of this rock, not bolts) rather than fixed hardware. You do not rappel from the summit block itself: parties protect the short scramble down from it to the top station with a handline, and there is a further rappel station down in the approach gully used to regain packs. The first two rappels go on a single rope, but the last is a full double-rope rappel needing two 70 m ropes — a single 60 m rope will not complete this descent, and 70 m ropes are what parties who have done it recommend. Bring an extra sling or two since anchor material on featureless granite here tends to be climber-placed webbing that may need refreshing. The final rappel lands back past the chockstone into the North-East Peak notch/gully, from which you downclimb and scramble the loose gully back down to the basin above Lake Ingalls, retracing the approach. Watch for loose rock in this gully on the way down, especially if other parties are above. As an alternative some climbers skip rappelling the direct line and instead do a short 4th-class downclimb from the East Peak summit block to link into the main peak's South Ridge descent/rappel line (shared with the standard Ingalls Peak South Ridge route), then talus back to Lake Ingalls.
hazards: routefinding among the Ingalls summits, especially locating the North/East col and chockstone
afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Stuart Range in summer
loose, exfoliating rock on the upper ridge and summit block
peridotite/serpentine rock is notably slippery when wet, dusty, or lichen-covered
exposed 3rd/4th-class scrambling on the approach to the notch

waysIn.name: Ingalls Way Trail, Lake Ingalls and the North–East col gully
waysIn.season: July through September once the pass switchbacks melt out; microspikes and an axe are worth carrying into July in a heavy snow year.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Ingalls Way Trail #1390 north beside the creek on an old mining-road grade. At the signed fork bear right onto #1390 where the Esmeralda Basin trail stays low and left, and at the second junction stay left where the Longs Pass trail branches east. Steady switchbacks through open larch lead to Ingalls Pass; cross it, drop slightly and follow cairns and boot track around the basin rather than giving up height, then climb a large steep boulder field to Lake Ingalls. Filter there — nothing above the lake holds water. A climbers' path skirts the east shore and heads up-basin toward the notch between the main summit and the horn-shaped East Peak.
hazards: The chossy central gully below the col is the main rockfall hazard on the approach — favour the clean slabs on the left
Several sub-gullies lead toward the notch and the largest, most direct one is the loosest and most dangerous
A great deal of loose rock on the route, so protection can end up run out on easy ground
Snow and ice on the upper trail switchbacks into July
The descent uses three rappel stations down the face — count them on the way up
No water above the lake

name: South Ridge
approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Lake Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/USFS Rd 9737), take the Ingalls Way Trail (#1390). At about 0.4 mile bear right at the junction onto Ingalls Way (Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 continues straight); at roughly 1.4 miles pass the Longs Pass junction. The trail climbs steadily through forest and open slopes to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft) at about 3.0-3.1 miles, the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary and your first full view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group. From the pass, drop slightly and traverse climbers'-left across open slabs and talus (a boot path braids through here; stay on durable surfaces where possible) for roughly another mile to Lake Ingalls (6,480 ft), about 4-4.5 miles and ~2,500-2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This is the last reliable water before the climb. From the lake's outlet/left (west) side, scramble up class 2-3 slabs and talus, aiming for the obvious cleft/notch splitting North Ingalls Peak from the main (South) summit, working up to about 7,100 ft. A short section of class 4 leads up a gully to a ledge system at the base of the ridge proper - this is where the roped climbing (pitch 1) begins. No creek fords are involved past the lake; the main approach hazards are loose talus/scree on the slabs above the lake and afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open ridge - start early. Total approach is commonly reckoned at 3-4 hours from the car.
descent: Descend by rappelling the South Ridge climbing line itself (or, for parties who diverge, the closely parallel Southwest Face). From the summit it is four rappels on a single 60 m rope, or three with two 60 m ropes, described here for two ropes: (1) a single-strand rappel down the uppermost pitch to a two-bolt anchor on a narrow ledge; (2) a full-length rappel (double-rope length, i.e. using the rope doubled) down to a large ledge/slung boulder near the top of pitch 2 - do not be tempted to skip straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel, since a crack just below the top anchor is notorious for wedging and stuck ropes have resulted; breaking it at the pitch-3 ledge avoids this; and (3) a final rappel from that ledge down to the base ledges/gully where the climb started. Anchors are a mix of fixed two-bolt stations and natural slung-boulder/horn anchors reinforced with webbing - carry a few extra feet of tat/webbing since the natural anchors get replaced periodically and can be tired. Below the last rappel, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach talus/slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
hazards: routefinding to gain the ridge
afternoon thunderstorms
crowds on a popular classic
loose rock in the approach gully and around the North/South notch
limited-to-no cell coverage in the Lake Ingalls basin

waysIn.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the slabs above the lake are clear; snow lingers below the notch into early summer
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead (about 4,240 ft) at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, FR 9737. A free self-issue Alpine Lakes wilderness permit is filled out at the register.

There are two forks and they are easily run together. The first comes at roughly a quarter to half a mile, where the old mine-road grade splits: bear right onto Ingalls Way #1390. Straight on is Esmeralda Basin #1394, a different valley. The second fork is higher, around 5,600 ft and roughly a mile and a half in: right climbs to Longs Pass, which is a viewpoint and the way toward Ingalls Creek and Stuart's south side, not a way to this climb. Stay left.

From there the trail traverses steadily to Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group come into view all at once. Continue about another mile to Lake Ingalls, roughly 6,400-6,480 ft and about 4 miles from the car. This is the last water.

From the lake, work up and climber's-left on Class 2-3 slabs, talus and boulders. Stay with the cairned line. Parties who leave it for a more direct-looking line get cliffed out; one party downclimbed past a waterfall to escape.
hazards: Cliffing out on the slabs above and beside the lake if you leave the cairned line for a direct one
Loose talus and scree in the approach gully with parties above
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed ridge — start early
A 60 m rope does not reach on the descent rappels, roughly fifteen feet short; carry a 70 m or doubles

waysIn.name: Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
waysIn.season: Same window; this is the branch to take if you are sleeping out, since camping at Lake Ingalls is prohibited
waysIn.notes:
Identical to Ingalls Pass. Just past the pass the trail splits and the right-hand branch is signed Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2. It drops into Headlight Basin, crosses Headlight Creek, and holds the established campsites and the reliable water. The main #1390 stays high along the rim of the basin and is the more direct line to the lake.

The two rejoin at a signed junction less than a quarter mile below Lake Ingalls, so this costs you a descent and a re-ascent in exchange for a legal camp and running water. Parties climbing the same day generally take the high line; parties camping take the low one.
hazards: Headlight Creek crossing
Braided use paths through the basin camps — stay on durable ground, this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness
Extra descent and re-ascent on the way out with a full pack
waysIn.whyThisWay: When spending the night, because camping at Lake Ingalls is not allowed and the basin has legal sites and water; day parties skip the extra drop and climb.

name: South Peak Scramble
approach: Park at the Esmeralda (Lake Ingalls) Trailhead at the end of the Teanaway River Road (FS-9737), roughly 4,300 ft, on the edge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Start on Ingalls Way Trail #1390: at about 0.4 mile a junction splits off the Esmeralda Basin Trail (stay right/uphill on Ingalls Way), and at roughly 1.5 miles the Longs Pass Trail #1229 branches right (continue straight, staying on #1390). The trail climbs steadily through open larch and subalpine slopes to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft) at about 3 miles, the first point with a clear view of Mount Stuart across the valley. From the pass the trail drops about a mile and several hundred feet into the basin to Lake Ingalls (~6,450 ft), the last reliable water source — carry water from here, as none is available higher. Leave the maintained trail at the lake and pick a way up talus, slabs, and boulders (an obvious dike/gully line is the easiest going) to the notch/col between Ingalls North and South Peaks; aim to pass just left of a small rock spire that sits in the saddle. Steep snow or verglas commonly lingers on the approach to the col into mid-summer, and an ice axe (sometimes crampons) is worth carrying through July. From the col, do not continue straight up the ridge crest — instead drop about 50 ft onto the west side of the ridge and climb one of several Class 2–3 gullies (~100 ft) back up to the crest, then follow the ridge over a mix of snow and blocky rock, with some exposure, to the South Peak summit. Round trip is roughly 11 miles with about 4,200 ft of cumulative gain. The route above the lake is unmarked and involves genuine route-finding on loose talus and boulders — this is the crux of the day for most parties, more so than any single move.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the ridge and the Class 2–3 gully back down to the North/South col, then pick your way back down the talus, slabs, and any lingering snow to Lake Ingalls, and rejoin Ingalls Way Trail #1390 back over Ingalls Pass to the Esmeralda Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble — no fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard South Peak route and the great majority of parties downclimb the entire route car-to-car in a day. Watch for loose rock and scree in the gully below the col (parties should stay bunched or descend one at a time to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below), and for the same lingering steep snow/ice near the col noted on the approach, which can make the downclimb more consequential than the ascent, especially early or late season. Some parties in icy conditions choose to sling a natural rock horn or block near the col and back up the short Class 3 step with a hand line or short rappel for extra security, but this is a personal-judgment call, not a standard part of the route, and no such anchor is left in place. The steep dusty climbers' path from the col is slick and a snow patch can linger across it into August; boulders beside it grip better than the dust.
hazards: routefinding to the summit block, especially reversing the route in whiteout or late-day cloud
exposed high-Class-3/low-Class-4 move on the summit block with brief but real exposure
loose rock in the ridge gullies below the col
early-season snow, thin snow bridges, and melted-out holes in the descent gully (reported into June)
afternoon thunderstorms common in July-August; exposed ridge and summit block offer no lightning shelter

waysIn.name: Ingalls Way Trail to Lake Ingalls and the North–South col
waysIn.season: July through September. Steep snow or verglas commonly lingers on the approach to the col into midsummer, so an axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying through July.
waysIn.notes: Follow Ingalls Way Trail #1390 from the road-end trailhead: bear right and uphill at the signed fork where the Esmeralda Basin trail drops away left, carry straight on where the Longs Pass trail branches right, and climb steady switchbacks through open larch to Ingalls Pass. From the crest the trail drops into the basin and contours to Lake Ingalls, giving back a few hundred feet. Two tracks cross the basin and rejoin; the more maintained of them avoids the Headlight Creek crossing. Fill and filter at the lake, because nothing higher holds water. Leave the maintained trail there and work up talus, slabs and boulders toward the saddle between the North and South Peaks.
hazards: Unmarked route-finding on loose talus and boulders above the lake — the real crux of the day for most parties
Steep lingering snow just below the saddle into midsummer
Severe drop-offs on the west side of the ridge
Loose rock in the short west-side gullies, which land on anyone beneath — move one at a time
No water above the lake

name: Standard Route (Northeast summit via South Gully and East Ridge)
approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~700 ft) — the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the closed roadbed, getting around the washed-out section on a riverside bypass. Several miles up, an unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs very steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon: roughly 3,300 ft in about 2 miles, choked with blowdown in its lower part and with some hands-on scrambling higher up, past a small creekside bench near 3,100 ft, to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft, the usual camp (a wilderness permit is needed and the lake is a quota area). From the lake, head north into barren Avalanche Canyon on a faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches to the broad couloir below the Thumb, where the South Chute of Mount Constance and the South Gully of Inner Constance part ways. A much longer alternative follows the closed road to its old end, climbs the Constance Pass Trail and crosses Crystal Pass into the head of Avalanche Canyon; it avoids the Lake Constance path's steep lower section. Expect a 2–3 day trip either way.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: scramble back down the East Ridge to the notch, downclimb or rappel the short rock step into the gully, then descend the discontinuous snow finger and the South Defile, watching for moats on both sides and for snow blocks that loosen as the day warms. Where the snow is firm and runs out safely, the lower couloir can be plunge-stepped or glissaded. Loose rock is a hazard the whole way off the summit, so keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line. From the broad couloir below the Thumb, walk back down Avalanche Canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' path and the closed Dosewallips Road to the washout.
hazards: Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
Exposed roped climbing including a steep, committing chimney/roof section ('cave of despair' in trip reports)
Easy to be drawn onto the wrong (southwest) summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
Deep moats bordering the snow finger in the South Gully/defile, requiring repeated stemming between snow and rock to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the gully as the day warms — a documented incident involved a refrigerator-size block breaking loose and striking a climber

waysIn.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
waysIn.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range

waysIn.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
waysIn.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
waysIn.whyThisWay: To avoid the steep, blowdown-choked lower Lake Constance climbers' trail, for parties willing to trade about eight extra miles and a two or three day trip for easier tread.

name: West Ridge
approach: Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead/group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first ~4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed/trail at easy grades along Goodell Creek (roughly 500 to 1,600 ft), crossing the creek and passing the last reliable flowing water around 1,600 ft — fill up here, because the trail goes dry above this point. A cairned/stone-arrow junction (sometimes marked, sometimes not) sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free climbers' boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting, root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades — widely described by parties as the crux of the whole approach. The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft, where you pick up meadows, slabs, and (often) snow, and make a rising traverse north/northeast toward a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically made just below this saddle in Terror Creek Basin (the standard Nelson & Potterfield-endorsed camp), a popular and sometimes crowded bivy with views of the Southern Pickets. From camp, the route to the base of the climb continues across heather and snow slopes trending north/northwest, losing a little elevation to cross the outlet drainage from a small tarn just SE of the McMillan Spires, then regaining ground on slabs and snow up to the edge of Terror Glacier. The glacier crossing below Inspiration's south side is low-angle but genuinely and heavily crevassed — rope up; snow bridges are usually adequate in normal season but should be checked, and parties should carry a rack for crevasse rescue. Total car-to-base is roughly 7 miles and 6,000+ ft of gain, typically taking most of a day; expect a long, steep, hot slog with real route-finding on the boot path and no water for the last ~3,500 ft of the climb to camp.
descent: The standard descent from the summit goes down the West Ridge crest itself, then finishes down Inspiration's South Face — it is not a walk-off. Most recent parties (e.g. a well-documented July 2024 ascent) report roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge on a single 60-70m rope, using a mix of fixed slings/rap rings left by prior parties (quality varies — some stations have been found tattered and worth backing up or replacing) and natural nut/cam anchors built on the spot. After the ridge raps, parties briefly stow the rope and downclimb/scramble 3rd-4th class terrain to a notch, from which roughly 9 more single-rope rappels descend the South Face to the Terror Glacier, for a total in the neighborhood of 12-14 rappels overall — the final rappel often takes the full length of the doubled rope to reach flat glacier snow. Some parties instead descend the full length of the West Ridge on a doubled/twin-rope system, using longer double-rope rappels off natural gear (solid nut placements) to cut the total rappel count to around 7, bypassing the separate South Face section — either line is used depending on party preference and rope setup. Watch for loose, rockfall-prone rock on the traversing stations (some raps go sideways, not straight down, to reach the next anchor and to dodge fall lines), stay alert for hard-to-spot anchor stations, and re-rope for glacier travel the instant you're back on the Terror Glacier at the bottom. From the glacier, reverse the approach: back across the crevassed glacier and slabs to Terror Basin camp, then down the steep boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead — parties frequently finish this exit in the dark, with some trip reports noting arrival at camp or the car well after nightfall.
hazards: crevassed Terror Glacier crossing and moat at the toe of the ridge, worse late season
'The Barrier' route-finding if continuing to/from Crescent Creek Basin — loose ledges or moats depending on which crossing is used
long, steep, unmaintained boot path on the approach (no switchbacks, tree-root 4th class sections)
rockfall from parties above on the shared West Ridge descent line
remoteness — no cell coverage, multi-day self-rescue distance

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and the stone-arrow boot path to Terror Basin, then the crevassed Terror Glacier to the bergschrund below the west end of the peak
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first roughly 4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed at easy grades from about 500 to 1,600 ft, crossing the creek and passing the last reliable flowing water around 1,600 ft. Fill up there; the trail is dry above.

A cairned stone-arrow junction, sometimes marked and sometimes not, sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades. Parties widely describe this as the crux of the whole approach.

The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft into meadows, slabs and often snow, and a rising traverse north-northeast leads to a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically just below it in Terror Creek Basin.
hazards: A heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing below the peak's south side; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
A bergschrund and a moat at the base that open through the season
Compact rock with scarce placements on the lower pitches
Loose blocks on the lower ledges
No water for the last 3,500 ft of the climb to camp
A rappel descent of 12-14 stations, with traversing raps that are rockfall-prone and stations that are hard to spot

name: Northwest Ridge / South Face
approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse. Beyond the pavement the last stretch of the forest road to the trailhead is long, washboarded gravel; a high-clearance car is more comfortable.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the loose Class 3 upper south face and the exposed ledge/cliff-band notch back to the northwest ridge, then follow the ridge crest back toward the Old Snowy–Ives col. From the col, most parties either (a) drop directly southwest through the scree/talus basin to regain the PCT — faster but the loosest, choss-iest line, or (b) traverse back over to Old Snowy Mountain and descend its established south-ridge boot path to the PCT near the Packwood Glacier bench, which avoids the worst loose rock directly below Ives' summit block. Either way, once back on the PCT, retrace it south to the Snowgrass Trail #96 junction and follow Snowgrass Trail #96 back down through Upper/Lower Snowgrass Flat and the Goat Creek crossing to the trailhead. This is entirely a scramble walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are involved or needed on this route. Primary descent hazards are the same loose talus/scree encountered on the ascent (higher consequence going downhill) and lingering snow/ice in the col and on the ridge crest into early-mid summer; a short glissade or scree-ski of the basin below the col is a common (optional) shortcut for the descent when snow-free.
hazards: exposure on the crest
afternoon thunderstorms
lingering snowfields and a glacier moat crossing near the Old Snowy-Ives col into July
off-trail routefinding with no maintained summit trail

waysIn.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
waysIn.season: Roughly late Jul through mid-Sep, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out
waysIn.notes: Start at the Snowgrass trailhead at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source. Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction, follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot. Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.
hazards: Loose, unconsolidated talus and scree with higher consequence on the descent
Chossy volcanic andesite on the summit south face
An exposed narrow ledge traverse below the summit, reached by downclimbing
Lingering snowfields and a moat crossing near the col into July
Off-trail route-finding with no maintained summit path
Exposure to afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest

name: Nohokomeen Glacier and Headwall
approach: From SR 20 milepost 138, park at the East Bank Trailhead (~1,800 ft) and descend briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek. Follow the East Bank Trail — mostly flat and fast — roughly 8 miles north along Ross Lake to the May Creek camp. (Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will drop parties on the eastern shore and is a legitimate way to skip most of the trail; check current rates and schedule directly with the resort.) At May Creek leave the trail and climb steeply east, loosely ascending between the creeks on the west side of Jack Mountain. Cliff bands begin around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails; snow generally appears around 4,800-5,000 ft. About 3 miles of this off-trail work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe. Strong parties push a second camp onto the upper glacier around 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably. Before the highway opens, parties have biked about 4 miles from the MP 134 gate to the trailhead and continued on foot or ski.
descent: There is no rappel line — the standard descent is to downclimb what you climbed, ideally in your own steps. Reverse the corniced summit ridge carefully, then face-in downclimb the headwall; parties that are not comfortable simul-downclimbing 50-60 degree snow lower each other off buried pickets on the steepest 100 m or so. Recross the bergschrund at the same bridge you used on the way up, and be aware that it will be softer and less trustworthy than it was in the morning. Descend the glacier roped, aiming to be off the snow before it crusts up or, in spring, before afternoon warming makes the lower slopes unstable. From the glacier toe, retrace the bushwhack down through the cliff bands to camp — this is genuinely hard to navigate in the dark and several parties have relied on GPS to find their line back through the timber. Reported summit-to-camp times run from about 2.5 hours (fast, in good steps) to considerably longer. From camp it is the 3-mile descent to May Creek and 8 miles of flat trail back to the car.
hazards: Crevasse fall on the Nohokomeen Glacier, which is heavily crevassed below its midpoint.
Bergschrund crossing on a single snow bridge, worsening with warmth and season.
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a 700-800 ft face of 50-60 degree snow, particularly once the sun is on it.
Cornice failure on the north-facing summit ridge.
A long unroped fall is the consequence of a slip anywhere on the headwall - self-arrest on 55-60 degree snow is unreliable.
Extreme remoteness: 11 miles from the road, no cell coverage, and a multi-day evacuation for any injury.

waysIn.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
waysIn.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
waysIn.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb east, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
hazards: Steep, brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to descend than to climb; a GPS track helps in the dark
Crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, heavily crevassed below midpoint and thinly bridged late season
Bergschrund crossing on a single snow bridge that softens with warmth
700-800 ft headwall of 50-60 degree snow: avalanche and wet-slide hazard once the sun is on it; long unroped fall if you slip
Cornice failure on the north-facing summit ridge
Rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
Eleven miles from the road: no cell coverage, a multi-day evacuation, and a two to four day commitment

waysIn.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
waysIn.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
waysIn.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
hazards: Fixed boat pickup times on a lake with no road out; build slack into the plan
Arriving late can mean the cliff-banded timber belt is done in the dark, where passages are found by eye
Steep brushy cliff-banded timber above the shore, far worse to descend than to climb
Crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, heavily crevassed below midpoint
Bergschrund crossing on a single snow bridge, and 50-60 degree snow on the headwall with avalanche and wet-slide hazard
Cornice failure on the summit ridge
No reliable communication once off the lake; a multi-day evacuation
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the boat service is running, usually from about early June, and a party wants to skip the trail miles and accepts a booked pickup time.

waysIn.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
waysIn.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
waysIn.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
waysIn.whyThisWay: In late winter or early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow; the road to the trailhead is covered by bike or skis first.

name: North Ridge
approach: No turn-by-turn approach is published. The north flank of Jack Mountain is reached from the Ross Lake East Bank Trail, which begins at the East Bank Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 138 (~1,800 ft); Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will also drop parties at points along the eastern shore, which shortens the trail walking considerably. Devils Creek is the main north-side drainage and the East Bank Trail crosses it. From wherever you leave the trail, expect a steep, brushy, cliff-banded climb through timber to reach open ground and the base of the ridge — on the Nohokomeen side, the same belt of terrain has cliff bands starting around 3,200 ft, threaded on game trails to reach snow near 4,800-5,000 ft. Treat the approach as exploratory: study current imagery and plan the line before committing. In July, take the lake boat to the Devils Creek landing and walk about two miles of shoreline to the Devils Creek bridge; fill up there, then climb the game trail just south of the bridge. The next water is a tarn near 5,700 ft (a pool on point 6,486 early in the month).
descent: The recorded modern practice is to traverse over the summit and descend the East Ridge (Grade II, Class 4), which puts you back on the eastern side of the mountain. That means downclimbing sustained Class 4 loose rock with occasional improvised rappels off slung blocks — carry tat and a few nuts, since there is no fixed gear on either ridge. Reversing the North Ridge and the Nohokomeen Glacier is possible and considerably easier than the East Ridge, but brings the added problem of finding the correct line back down brushy, cliff-banded terrain to the East Bank Trail, which is hard in the dark. Whichever you choose, scout it before you climb and record a GPS track on the way up through the timber; several north-side parties on this mountain have depended on one to get home. The South Face is a third exit but strands you on the opposite side of the peak from any northern camp.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the Hozameen Group bedrock
Remote location with a long, difficult retreat

waysIn.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft far more often by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of the East Bank Trail walk from SR 20. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout with little that holds protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a low fifth-class pitch where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late season
Very remote, several days from a road with no realistic quick rescue; the usual East Ridge descent is sustained loose class 4

waysIn.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek
waysIn.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open. The walk is seven or eight flat miles.
hazards: Several flat miles of lake trail each way before the climb begins: a long, committing trip with no quick way out
Steep forest with cliff bands above May Creek, hard to navigate in the dark and far worse to descend
Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe; crevasses low on the glacier
Loose, fractured rock on the ridge with little that holds protection
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and the snow traverse below the summit tower
Very remote with no realistic quick rescue
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the water taxi is not running or booked, such as before early June, or a party prefers not to depend on a pickup; costs several hours of flat walking each way.

name: South Face / Southeast Ridge
approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (about 16 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~1,900ft), cross Canyon Creek on a log/plank crossing (can wash out in high water, check current conditions) and follow the Crater Lake/Jackita Ridge Trail (FST 738) as it climbs steeply through forest — roughly 3,400ft of gain in about 4 miles — to the Crater Mountain Trail (FST 746) junction near McMillan Park. Take FST 746 toward Crater Lake (~2,000ft of gain, about 2.3 hours in); this stretch has long, hot, dry switchbacks with no reliable water, so carry what you need from Canyon Creek. Around 6,700–7,200ft, leave the maintained trail and traverse toward the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak (Crater Mountain Saddle, ~7,200ft, roughly 4.2 hours from the trailhead). From the saddle, descend/traverse the Jerry Glacier — often patchy or nearly bare by late summer but still crevassed enough in early season to warrant crampons and a rope — to Jerry Lakes basin (5,900–6,550ft, ~6.4 hours in). From Jerry Lakes, traverse a heather shelf to a 6,520ft notch/pass south of the lakes, then descend about 600ft into Crater Creek Basin through mild terrain and up to the 7,000ft shoulder that accesses the southeast ridge; most parties camp in the 6,000ft basin at Crater Creek Meadows, northwest of point 7,001 (~8.3 hours / roughly 11 miles from the car). On summit day, traverse west from camp across steep scree and dirt slopes below the south face to a landmark 'slinged boulder,' then find a left-slanting ramp that breaches the lower cliff band; a short Class 4 step leads to a hidden Class 3 chimney, above which roughly 1,000ft of Class 2–3 scrambling (with a stretch of exposed low-5th-class climbing and two informal belay stations noted near 8,000ft) gains the southeast ridge and summit block. Hazards throughout: fire-damaged forest sections near Jerry Lakes, loose rock and moats on the glacier margins, crevasse crossings, and significant route-finding difficulty locating the chimney/ramp system on the face.
descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the southeast ridge back to the top of the south face, then pick a descent line of gray rock ribs and gully rather than the loose 'bowling alley' gully used on the way up — marker ducks placed on the ascent are commonly used to relocate the correct line. The crux is getting back down through the cliff band via the hidden chimney and Class 4 step; the majority of parties downclimb this face-to-face, belaying weaker members through the chimney and avoiding rappels because of loose, debris-prone rock that can be kicked onto climbers below. At least one party describes a rappel option through this same cliff band as the sketchiest rappel on the route, warning that a 30m rope leaves you short and forces a further downclimb — so if you do rappel here, bring at least a 45m single rope (a 60m rope, or a double-rope rappel with two shorter ropes, gives real margin). Any anchor here is natural — a sling around a boulder or horn (the same 'slinged boulder' landmark used on the approach) rather than any fixed/bolted gear — so bring cord/webbing and rap rings to build or back up the anchor. From the base of the cliff band, continue down scree and dirt slopes back to the Crater Creek Meadows camp (roughly 4 hours from the summit), then reverse the full approach: back over the 6,520ft notch, across (or high above) the Jerry Glacier, over the Crater Mountain saddle, and down FST 746/738 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead. Some parties use an alternate descent via Jerry Lakes, Devil's Lake, and the East Crater Mountain lookout, dropping via a ledge system below the glacier to avoid crossing the Jerry Glacier entirely (about 6.6 hours back to the vehicle from the lakes area). Key descent hazards: significant rockfall/loose-rock risk on the downclimb (helmets essential, stagger climbers, avoid kicking debris on parties below), crevasse hazard re-crossing the glacier, and route-finding difficulty in whiteout or late-day conditions given how long and complex this descent is.
hazards: routefinding on a complex, largely featureless face
short exposed class 4 (occasional low 5th) steps
open crevasses crossing the toe of the Jerry Glacier on approach
afternoon thunderstorms, common July-August
long, remote multi-day approach with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
waysIn.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the very start, which has washed out
long waterless switchbacks on both trail sections
crevasses and moats on the Jerry Glacier, worse as a bare-ice slip hazard late in the season
fire-damaged forest and unstable ground near Jerry Lakes
loose rock on the face where holds pull off freely - keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked
