route-finding for the ramp and hidden chimney, which are hard to relocate on the descent

waysIn.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
waysIn.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
waysIn.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent. Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of Crater Creek Basin if you camp low
no water above the lakes or the meadows
exposed camps with weather coming over the crest
loose ground on the traverse under the face
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties wanting the meadow camp, which keeps running water later in the season and puts summit day on the right side of the notch, at the cost of a descent and re-ascent.

name: Southeast Ridge (Direct)
approach: Identical to the South Face route. Drive SR 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead (~1,900 ft) near milepost 141, ford Canyon Creek (the Trail #738 bridge is destroyed), and follow the McMillan Park-Jackita Ridge Trail up about 62 switchbacks and 3,900 ft to Crater Lake at the Crater Mountain Trail junction (3.7 mi). Leave the trail, traverse north under Crater Mountain to the ~7,200 ft Crater Mountain / Jerry Glacier saddle, descend steep neve and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the 6,550 ft saddle above Jerry Lakes and camp at the lakes (~6,400 ft) or at Crater Creek meadows (~6,000 ft). From camp, gain the southeast ridge at the 7,000-7,200 ft step; the ridge crest above is the route. Allow five hours minimum car-to-lakes light, or 8+ hours with overnight loads to the Crater Creek camp.
descent: The practical descent is the South Face. From the summit, reverse the short summit ridge and work down the face's gullies and ribs, aiming for the notch in the south ridge and then for the slung boulder that sits above the hidden chimney in the lower cliff band. Rappel the chimney (25-30 m), reverse the left-slanting ramp and the rising scree traverse east, and regain the 7,000-7,200 ft southeast ridge step, from which open slopes lead down to camp. Reversing the Direct itself would mean multiple rappels on loose greenstone with no fixed anchors and is not the normal choice. Getting home from camp still requires recrossing the Jerry Glacier and the 7,200 ft Crater Mountain saddle, or the alternative exit via Devils Lake and the East Crater Mountain lookout.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the Hozameen Group bedrock
Remote location with a long, difficult retreat

waysIn.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
waysIn.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, ford Canyon Creek - there is no bridge, and it runs high and hazardous in spring and early summer, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the start
crevasses and steep neve on the Jerry Glacier both ways
loose blocks on the crest - the rock on this mountain pulls off freely
sustained exposure with rappels needed to reverse the steps
a long committing position with a multi-hour retreat to camp

waysIn.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
waysIn.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
waysIn.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of the basin from the meadows camp
no water above the lakes or meadows
wind-exposed camps
loose ground on the climb back to the shoulder
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties wanting the meadow camp, which holds running water later in the season and starts summit day beneath the shoulder where the ridge is gained, after a descent and re-ascent.

name: Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir (East Ridge)
approach: Shares its start with the Northeast Buttress: from the Cascade Pass trailhead (~3,600 ft), descend briefly from the parking lot, cross the creek/river drainage, and work through brush and a terminal moraine to reach a permanent snowfield around 3,300 ft. It's one of the more compact approaches in the range, but the brush travel is unpleasant in the dark on an alpine-start day.
descent: Reverse the east ridge and descend the couloir, ideally while the snow remains firm, watching for rockfall and slide activity as the day warms.
hazards: avalanche and rockfall in the confined couloir
steep snow (continuous 30-50°) squeezed by the Sill Glacier for roughly 3,400 ft
crevasse hazard on the Sill Glacier, including a ~300 ft bottleneck section that narrows to 20-50 ft wide
the couloir becomes increasingly difficult and dangerous as crevasses open through the season — best treated as an early-season-only route
poor, loose rock (mossy, broken gneiss) on the East Ridge above the col
the long, route-finding east ridge with sustained exposure
wet slides and softening snow bridges as the day warms

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass trailhead to the couloir apron
waysIn.season: May-Jun, while the Sill Glacier snow is still continuous
waysIn.notes:
Effectively no approach at all. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft, walk back down the road — accounts range from a quarter mile to just under a mile depending on where you drop in — then descend a dirt and brush embankment into the valley and cross the Cascade River. In spring the river is often still snow-covered where you cross.

Over the terminal moraine and a snowfield, and within about twenty minutes of dropping off the road you are putting crampons on at the apron at roughly 3,300 ft. From there it is about 3,000 ft of continuous booting to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

In a big snow year Cascade River Road may be gated well below the trailhead — one ski party found it gated at mile 18 but snow-free to the last hairpin, and used bikes for the road section. Budget for that possibility rather than assuming you can drive to the end.

Season is the whole decision on this route. Early season is when the snow is continuous. As the Sill Glacier breaks up, the snow in the couloir goes discontinuous where it narrows near the hanging glacier and the breaks turn into a series of separate problems; by mid to late summer it is broken and considerably more hazardous.
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier over the whole couloir
Discontinuous snow where the couloir narrows, worsening through the season
Cascade River crossing — snow-bridged in spring, a ford later
Spring wet-slide activity in a 3,000 ft snow chute
Road may be gated miles below the trailhead in a heavy snow year

name: South Ridge
approach: Start at the Denny Creek Trailhead (~2,280 ft), reached via Forest Road 58 (Denny Creek Road) off I-90 Exit 47. From the trailhead, follow Denny Creek Trail #1014 north/east up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles the trail crosses Denny Creek at the 'Slippery Slab' — smooth cascading bedrock and pools that are the last easy, reliable water source before the climb steepens. Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus/boulder slopes, and switchbacks up to Hemlock Pass (~3.8 miles, ~4,600 ft), where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction (the right/east fork continues toward Lower Tuscohatchie Lake). Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake basin (~4.3-4.5 miles, ~4,550 ft) below Chair and Kaleetan Peaks — good campsites and the last dependable water before the summit push. From the lake outlet, leave the maintained trail and follow a well-defined but unmaintained climbers' path that heads steeply northwest, gaining Kaleetan Knoll (Peak 5,700) through subalpine trees, heather, and talus. From the knoll the boot path drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle that separates Peak 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge; cairns mark the crossing but route-finding can be tricky in cloud or early-season snow. Regain the ridge at the saddle and follow the boot path north, just below/along the crest, for a few hundred yards to the base of an obvious gully/ledge system splitting Kaleetan's south face — this is the standard finish, roughly 400-600 vertical feet of Class 2-3 scrambling on loose, exfoliating rock, exiting onto a short summit ridge with one more brief scramble to the true summit (6,259-6,260 ft). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is about 9-10 km (matching the 19.3 km round trip) with about 4,500 ft of total gain. Key hazards: the summit gully and upper shoulder hold snow well into early summer — recent parties often describe needing an ice axe and light crampons on the northwest-facing finish into June/July; the rock on the upper peak is loose throughout, and exposure increases near the top; and the talus traverse below the Kaleetan Knoll saddle has no continuous trail, so cairn-following and route-finding judgment (especially in poor visibility) are required.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — the standard South Ridge route is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling. Downclimb the summit gully/ledge system carefully; loose, exfoliating rock is the primary hazard on the way down, so descend one climber at a time through the gully to avoid knocking rock onto partners below. From the base of the gully, regain the saddle, re-cross the west-facing talus bowl below Peak 5,700 (following cairns), go back up and over Kaleetan Knoll, and drop down to Melakwa Lake. From the lake, follow Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 back up and over Hemlock Pass, then down Denny Creek Trail #1014 to the trailhead. In early-season conditions, when the gully still holds snow, parties often downclimb facing in or plunge-step an adjacent snow tongue with an ice axe rather than downclimb bare rock; a short hand-line or sling-and-rappel off a natural horn/block is occasionally improvised by parties uncomfortable with the exposed, loose downclimb, but this is not standard practice and there is no documented fixed or bolted rappel anchor on this route.
hazards: loose rock at the 'White Ledges' section and summit gully - test holds before weighting
ridge crest exposure on the upper South Ridge (Class 3)
lingering snow in the summit gully often into July, requiring an ice axe
afternoon thunderstorms, common on Cascade summer scrambles - start early and watch the sky

waysIn.name: Denny Creek to Melakwa Lake and the south ridge
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; the northwest-facing finish holds snow into June or July
waysIn.notes:
Denny Creek trailhead (about 2,280 ft) via Forest Road 58 off I-90 exit 47. Take Denny Creek Trail #1014 up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles it crosses Denny Creek at the Slippery Slab — smooth cascading bedrock and pools, and the last easy reliable water before the climb steepens.

Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus, and switchbacks to Hemlock Pass around 3.8 miles and 4,600 ft, where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction. Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake at roughly 4,550 ft — good campsites, and the last dependable water before the summit push.

From the lake, cross the outlet stream and pick up the well-defined but unmaintained climbers' bootpack on the ridge to the west (your left as you look up the lake). It climbs steeply through subalpine trees, heather and talus onto Kaleetan Knoll, Point 5,700.

The path then goes over that first prominence and drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle separating Point 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge. Cairns mark that crossing. There is no continuous tread here, and the cairns are the first thing to disappear in cloud or early-season snow.
hazards: loose, exfoliating rock throughout the summit gully and upper ridge
snow lingering on the northwest-facing finish into June or July - trip reports carry axe and light traction
no continuous trail on the talus traverse below the saddle - cairn-following only, and useless in cloud
increasing exposure near the top
no dependable water above Melakwa Lake

name: North Face
approach: Start from the Hairpin turnout on SR-20 (elev. ~5,150 ft), about 1 mile east of/beyond Washington Pass on the North Cascades Highway. From the large pullout, pick up the climber's trail that switchbacks up into the valley to the southeast — it's faint and boulder-hopping at first through talus and sandy gullies (look for cairns; the tread firms up after the first quarter mile), passing a small dried-up tarn. Stay along the right-hand (west) edge of the timber as you gain the valley headwall. This climber's path/trail gains roughly 1,500 ft over about 1.5 miles to Kangaroo Pass, a broad, view-filled saddle that's the key approach landmark (budget 1–1.5 hrs from the car at a moderate pace; there is no reliable water along this stretch, so carry what you need from the trailhead). From Kangaroo Pass, do not drop straight down the far side — instead contour/traverse south along the base of the slabs descending from Wallaby Peak, losing about 20 ft below the level of the pass, to pick up a good, well-cairned climber's trail. Follow this trail close beneath the slabs, staying below all the major slab bands, traversing toward Kangaroo Temple until you reach a gully system leading up to the high notch at the base of the North Face (about 200 ft below the notch an obvious bench/trail also splits off right toward the Northwest Face for parties headed there instead). Ascend the gully to the notch, which is the start of the North Face route. Hazards are mostly route-finding (the boulder-field tread disappears and reappears repeatedly before the pass) plus loose talus/scree underfoot and, early season, potential snow/ice in the approach gully warranting an ice axe. Total car-to-base time is typically 1.5–2.5 hours; guided/club trip reports cite 7–8 hours car-to-summit-and-back for the full outing.
descent: Descend by rappel back down the North Face line to the notch, then reverse the approach trail to the Hairpin. From the summit, the standard descent is three single-rope rappels using a 60 m rope: rap 1 from chain anchors at the top of the North Face; rap 2 from a second set of chains (or, per some trip reports, an alternate flake-and-tree anchor roughly 30 ft below/near those chains) — note a 50 m rope only just barely reaches this station, so a 60 m rope is strongly preferred; the descent line goes over a sharp lip onto vertical face, so manage rope-pull and stance carefully. Rap 3 from the next station lands you on down-climbable low-5th/4th-class terrain just above the high notch where the route began — from there it's an easy scramble/walk back down into the notch and gully. The stations are fixed, but their rigging varies (chains at some, bolts with slung cord at others), so inspect each one before loading; no anchor building should be needed. Once back at the notch, reverse the approach: descend the gully, pick up the climber's trail along the base of the slabs back to Kangaroo Pass, then follow the boulder-field/forest climber's trail down to the Hairpin trailhead. Watch for other parties queued at the rap stations — this is a popular Mountaineers/club route and backups at the anchors are common on weekends.
hazards: airy/exposed corner on P3
awkward step-down and flared crack near the belay tree
approach over faint cairned boulder fields
loose, dirty summit gully below the north-ridge notch often holds snow or verglas into June
the P3 belay tree is old and weathered — back it up with gear rather than relying on it alone
very popular route: expect other parties on the pitches and at the 3 rappel stations; watch for rockfall or dropped gear from climbers above and avoid rappelling onto parties below
The standard descent rappel reaches a blocky, loose first ledge; belayers should avoid standing directly below the leader on the approach gully

waysIn.name: The Hairpin turnout, the boulder-field path to Kangaroo Pass, then the traverse below Wallaby's slabs to the high notch
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start from the Hairpin turnout on SR-20 at about 5,150 ft, roughly a mile east of Washington Pass. From the large pullout, pick up the climber's trail that switchbacks up into the valley to the southeast; it is faint and boulder-hopping at first through talus and sandy gullies, with cairns, and the tread firms up after the first quarter mile, passing a small dried-up tarn. Stay along the right-hand, west, edge of the timber as you gain the valley headwall.

This path gains roughly 1,500 ft over about 1.5 miles to Kangaroo Pass, a broad view-filled saddle that is the key approach landmark; budget 1-1.5 hours from the car. No reliable water on this stretch. Car-to-base is typically 1.5-2.5 hours.
hazards: Route-finding where the boulder-field tread disappears and reappears repeatedly before the pass
Loose talus and scree underfoot throughout
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully, warranting an ice axe
A 50 m rope barely reaches the second rappel station; the descent line goes over a sharp lip onto vertical face
Queues at the rap stations; this is a popular club route and weekend backups are common
No reliable water on the approach

name: Southwest Gully
approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 (milepost ~151, roughly 30 miles east of Newhalem / ~45 miles from Marblemount). Follow Easy Pass Trail (Green Trails Mt. Logan No. 49) 3.5-3.6 miles and about 2,700-3,000 ft of gain to Easy Pass at 6,550 ft — figure 2-3 hours. The trail crosses Granite Creek on a footlog near the start, climbs through about 2 miles of hemlock/silver-fir forest, then breaks into open avalanche meadows and crosses Easy Pass Creek three times before the final push to the pass; steep snow can linger on this upper section well into July and an ice axe is recommended into early summer. From the pass, drop down the North Cascades National Park side to the end of the first switchback, where a faint, easy-to-miss climbers' path breaks off onto Ragged Ridge — this junction is unmarked and is the most commonly botched route-finding point on the whole approach; if you don't spot the boot path, head off-trail toward the ridge anyway. From there, sidehill northwest across scree, talus, grass and blocky terrain at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft along the south side of the ridge (about an hour), crossing one notable waterfall/stream beneath Mesahchie Peak around 6,500 ft on an easy bench — this is the one water crossing of consequence on the traverse and also a reliable water source. Continue to the basin/shoulder at roughly 6,600-6,870 ft just south of the Katsuk-Mesahchie col, known as Ragged Ridge Camp (only two workable flat tent sites; good water draining the basin). An NPS backcountry permit is required to camp here. From camp, gain a further 200-600 ft to a saddle/bench on the ridge descending from Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short stretch of 4th-class scrambling near the top — then locate the leftward-trending Southwest Gully high on the peak, which runs up toward a mushroom-shaped summit block. Low in the gully, bypass a waterfall by staying on its left (west) side on loose, 'kitty-litter' scree (Class 3). In early season (before roughly July) the entire gully holds steep snow to 45 degrees and demands an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing technique. Given the ~19.3 km round-trip distance, this is realistically an overnight approach (roughly 5 miles and about 3,000 ft to camp) rather than a single-push dayhike for most parties.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the Southwest Gully's Class 3 loose scree, staying left/west of the waterfall low in the gully, back to the ridge saddle/bench, then pick your way down scree to Ragged Ridge Camp. From camp, reverse the roughly 6,600-6,800 ft sidehill traverse (crossing back over the stream/waterfall bench beneath Mesahchie Peak) to regain the base of Easy Pass, climb back over the pass, and descend Easy Pass Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard Southwest Gully route; no fixed anchors, bolted stations, or rappel slings are mentioned in any route description or trip report found. The main descent hazards are loose rock and scree underfoot (rockfall risk onto anyone below in the gully or on the ridge traverse), the same route-finding difficulty relocating the faint climbers' trail junction near Easy Pass's first switchback, and, in early season, downclimbing or glissading steep snow in the gully (45+ degrees in spots) which requires an ice axe and good snow skills.
hazards: class 4 crux gully with loose 'kitty litter' rock, especially where the route bypasses a waterfall low in the gully on its left (west) side
huge exposure down the north face off the final ~50 ft summit block — described by multiple trip reports as needing extreme care
notoriously loose, rotten rock across Ragged Ridge generally (granite/slate) — real rockfall risk to parties below
difficult route-finding through the gully/rib system above the 7,400 ft bench; no maintained trail
no cell coverage in the basin/approach; remote, multi-hour evacuation if injured

waysIn.name: Ragged Ridge Camp to the waterfall at 7,760 ft
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, climb 200 to 600 ft to the saddle and bench on the ridge running down off Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short 4th-class stretch near the top. From there hike a short way up the broad ridge, then veer left and make an ascending traverse below the cliffs. Past the waterfall the going crosses the basin on softer ground, then continues on a slight rising traverse following small marmot trails and rocky ledges through a run of ribs and gullies. A backcountry permit is required to camp at the basin.
hazards: The gully is incredibly loose — every handhold needs testing
Continuous snow to 45 degrees in the gully before roughly July; axe, crampons and real snow technique
The final fifty feet to the summit sits above a long drop down the north face
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully — do not stack up

name: Standard Scramble (off the PCT)
approach: From I-90 Exit 52 (West Snoqualmie Pass), the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT northbound) lot sits just off the exit ramp on a short dirt spur (Northwest Forest Pass required; the ~50-car lot fills early on weekends). From the trailhead (~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north through second-growth forest: a first switchback at 0.6 mi (3,230 ft), a switchback pair at 1.5 mi (3,690 ft), and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at 2.0 mi (3,830 ft), where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases downhill slightly to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 mi (3,775 ft) - stay right/straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two stream crossings near this junction (plus a small waterfall/seasonal creek around 2.25 mi) are the last reliable water and can run high and tricky in early season. Beyond the junction the PCT climbs steadily under Kendall Peak's west flank through open talus and heather (Kendall Gardens, roughly mile 5, best wildflowers in August), then switchbacks directly below the peak (~5.5-6 mi, ~5,100-5,200 ft). Watch here for a large, distinctive stump partially blocking the left side of the trail at about 5,200 ft; roughly 15 feet beyond it, a boot path forks right (east) off the PCT and climbs straight uphill - this is the turnoff for the standard scramble. Leave the PCT and follow this boot path for the final ~400-500 vertical feet to the northernmost (highest) summit; it's steep, loose dirt and scree with occasional hands-on Class 2 moves, similar in character to the summit pitch on nearby Bandera Mountain. There is no water past the Commonwealth Creek crossings, so carry what you need for the upper mountain. Parties who overshoot the stump/bootpath and continue on the PCT to where it crosses the ridge on the east side can alternatively scramble the ridge crest south to the true summit, but that line is Class 3-4 with abundant loose rock and notably more exposed and dangerous than the bootpath - it is not the standard route. Snow can linger in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse below Kendall Gardens well into early summer, so check current conditions before a spring trip.
descent: Descend the same way you climbed: back down the loose dirt-and-talus boot path to the stump on the PCT, then follow the PCT south/back roughly 5.5-6 miles to the Exit 52 trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no technical rappelling anywhere on the standard route (rappels: 0). The boot path is the steepest and loosest stretch of the whole outing - descending it means kicking down through scree and dirt with hands often needed for balance on Class 2 terrain, and parties should space out or downclimb one at a time in its narrower sections to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below. If any snow remains on the boot path or on the PCT traverse near Kendall Gardens (which drops off steeply to the west), carry an ice axe and know how to self-arrest - a slip or postholing misstep on that exposed traverse is reportedly genuinely dangerous. Do not improvise a shortcut off the ridge or peak's other gullies to save time: parties who left the established bootpath/PCT line have run into unexpected rock bands, avalanche chutes, and difficult creek crossings trying to find a more direct descent. Stick to the boot path and PCT both up and down.
hazards: Kendall Katwalk itself: a narrow, exposed trail blasted into a cliff face; a 64-year-old hiker fell roughly 300 ft to her death here on September 5, 2018, and it remains a well-documented fall-fatality site
steep snow on the Katwalk approach and summit gullies into June-July in high-snow years, with avalanche potential earlier in the season
loose, 'choosy' rock ('kitty litter') on the boot path and near the summit block
off-trail route-finding on the unmarked boot path, especially in fog, whiteout, or fresh snow

waysIn.name: PCT north to the stump at 5,200 ft, then the boot path east
waysIn.season: June to October; snow can linger in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse below Kendall Gardens into early summer
waysIn.notes:
From I-90 exit 52 the PCT northbound lot sits just off the ramp on a short dirt spur; a Northwest Forest Pass is required and the roughly 50-car lot fills early at weekends.

From about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through second growth: first switchback at 0.6 mile, a switchback pair at 1.5 miles, the wilderness boundary at 2.0 miles where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases slightly downhill to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 miles — stay right and straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two stream crossings near that junction are the last reliable water.

Beyond, the PCT climbs under Kendall Peak's west flank through open talus and heather — Kendall Gardens, around mile 5 — then switchbacks directly below the peak at about 5.5 to 6 miles and 5,100 to 5,200 ft.

About 7.4 km and 2,800 ft.
hazards: Steep, loose dirt and scree on the final boot path
Lingering snow in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse into early summer
The class 3-4 ridge alternative, more exposed and loose than the standard route, entered by accident if the stump is missed
No water above the Commonwealth Creek crossings

name: Southwest Slopes / Gully
approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (milepost ~151, elev. ~3,800 ft). Follow the Easy Pass Trail — a well-graded but relentless climb through old-growth forest and switchbacks along Easy Creek — for about 3.5-3.6 miles and roughly 2,800 ft of gain to Easy Pass itself (~6,550 ft), where the trail crests into open meadows with the first views of Fisher Basin and the Ragged Ridge crest. Do not descend the trail's switchbacks toward Fisher Creek on the far side; instead leave the maintained trail near the pass and begin a cross-country sidehill traverse west along the south side of the ridge, roughly holding the 6,600-6,700 ft contour. This stretch crosses several small gullies and minor buttresses on talus and heather benches, passes below a large basin under Mesahchie Col, and continues west for about another mile. Watch for a waterfall and a band of steep scree partway along that forces a ~200 ft descent to find a safe crossing point — this is the trickiest route-finding section of the approach and is easy to get cliffed out on if you traverse too high. The standard camp is a basin at ~6,600 ft south of Mesahchie Peak, roughly 5 hours and 5-6 miles of travel from the trailhead, with reliable water from snowmelt streams and the waterfall drainage nearby (water can dry up late season). From camp, gain about 800 ft to a bench around 7,400 ft and traverse west along that bench for roughly 2.5 hours toward the Kimtah/Thieves Peak col (~7,900 ft) and beyond, crossing broken granite and slate terrain the whole way — this is sustained, exposed, trail-less cross-country travel, not a simple hike, and route-finding skill at class 3-4 is essential. No reliable water past the basin camp in late season.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit gully back to the ~7,400 ft bench, then work back east along the south-slope traverse, staying on or near the outbound line (cairns mark the route in places) to bypass the Grotesque Gendarmes buttress (a short 4th-class downclimb with real exposure) before regaining the sidehill traverse back toward Easy Pass and the maintained trail. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no fixed rappel stations reported — one winter party downclimbed rather than rappelled because the upper mountain offered no obvious solid anchors, consistent with the loose/fractured granite and slate character of the terrain. A rope, a few slings, and gear for natural anchors (horns, chockstones) are worth carrying as a contingency for a short rappel around the gendarmes or a wet/icy gully, but the standard descent for this route is downclimbing, not rappelling. Main hazards: loose rock and 4th-class exposure at the gendarme bypass, potential snow/runout in the gully early season, and the same tricky waterfall/scree crossing on the return traverse that made the approach route-finding nontrivial — down-climbing steep scree in this section in worsening light or weather is the most commonly cited crux of the whole outing.
hazards: loose rock (granite and slate) in the gullies
route-finding among parallel gullies and a cliffy, cave-like traverse section
exposure near the summit
steep snow on the Easy Pass Trail's north-facing switchbacks into July
~250-300 ft airy class-4 down-climb around a prominent gendarme on the traverse
water sources in the gullies can dry up later in the season

waysIn.name: Ragged Ridge Camp and the red ledge
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, gain roughly 800 ft to a bench near 7,400 ft, then traverse west holding somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft. The traverse is an endless maze of ribs and gullies and you will cross easily over a dozen of them. The hardest section is a rib about halfway along: drop to around 7,200 ft and look for two ledges that give passage, at the cost of some elevation to regain and a short stretch of class 4. Where a line looks like the easiest way through, it usually goes. There is no reliable water past the basin camp late in the season.
hazards: Sustained exposed traversing on loose ribs and gullies
The class 4 downclimb and narrow gully at the halfway rib
A cliffy cave section on the ledge around 7,800 ft
Route-finding failure in cloud — the ribs are indistinguishable from one another

name: North Ridge
approach: From Marblemount on WA-20, drive the Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 19-21 miles (paved to roughly mile 10, then gravel/washboard) to the Eldorado trailhead (~2,150 ft). Cross the North Fork Cascade River and follow the unmaintained Eldorado climbers' trail through forest and a boulder field to treeline, then to Eldorado Basin/Roush Creek camps (~6,000-6,300 ft). Ascend the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the ~7,500-ft notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, traverse ~1.5 miles north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (7,800 ft), then continue easily to the nearby Klawatti-Austera Col (7,900 ft) to start the ridge.
descent: Downclimb the ridge crest back around The Smokestack via its west-side gully, return to the Klawatti-Austera Col, then to Klawatti Col. From there re-cross the Inspiration Glacier to the notch on Eldorado's East Ridge, descend the Eldorado Glacier, and follow the climbers' trail to the trailhead.
hazards: Exposure on narrow ridge sections.
Loose rock on ledge traverses near The Smokestack.

waysIn.name: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, when the crest and the connecting cols are snow-free enough to scramble
waysIn.notes:
Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,150 ft, then the standard Eldorado climbers' path: forest, boulder field, treeline, and camps in Eldorado Basin / Roush Creek around 6,000-6,300 ft. Climb the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge near 7,500 ft, then traverse roughly a mile and a half north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft.

Klawatti Col is not the start of this route. Continue past it, along a lobe of the McAllister Glacier under Klawatti Peak's west face, about 0.4 mile to the next break in the ridge — the Klawatti-Austera Col at about 7,900 ft. The scramble takes about an hour from that col, up to two hours if you count from Klawatti Col.
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration and the upper McAllister lobe
A moat at the Klawatti-Austera col that ranges from class 4 to class 5 depending on where you cross it
Exposure on narrow sections of the crest, where route-finding is what keeps the grade at third class
Loose rock on the ledge traverses around The Smokestack

name: Southeast Face / Klawatti Glacier
approach: From the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road (large gravel pullout at roughly mile 19, elev. ~2,100 ft), the hike begins by crossing the Cascade River on a log crossing — the exact log/spot shifts year to year and sometimes washes out, so scout up- and downstream if the reported crossing is gone. From the river, pick up the unmaintained but well-beaten Eldorado Creek climbers' path, which switchbacks steeply through timber and brush, gaining about 1,500 ft to a talus/boulder field around 4,000 ft. Stay climbers'-right through the boulders (cairn lines that trend left lead into cliffier terrain). Above the boulder field, a climbers' trail follows a rib up to a basin around 5,500-5,800 ft, from which you descend slightly into the Roush Creek drainage — the last reliable running water on the approach — before re-ascending to bivy sites around 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel: climb the Eldorado Glacier (crevasses present, worse late-season), then make the long, mostly-flat traverse east across the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (~7,800 ft), a broad saddle with good bivy sites on Klawatti Peak's south side. This ice-cap traverse is the navigational crux of the approach — whiteout is common, so carry a map/GPS track and be ready to navigate blind. From Klawatti Col, a short direct climb up the peak's south-facing flank reaches the base of the technical route (the bergschrund and short rock step). Figure roughly 7-8 miles and 6,500+ ft of gain one-way from trailhead to the base of the climb; most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip with a glacier camp rather than a car-to-car push.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line back down to Klawatti Col rather than continuing over the top on a different line. From the summit, downclimb the moderate 40-55° snow/ice slope back to the top of the short low-5th-class rock step that clears the bergschrund near the route's base. Multiple trip reports (including a 'white-knuckle' late-day retreat in worsening weather) describe this step being rappelled rather than downclimbed once the schrund has opened up, which is the norm by mid-to-late season. Expect one rappel of roughly 30m to get past the bergschrund and back onto the glacier — a doubled 60m rope is sufficient; no second rappel is typically needed. Anchors here are natural, not bolted: slung horns, chockstones, or a picket/deadman in snow, so carry a few slings/nuts and inspect any existing tat before weighting it. Below the schrund, re-cross the Inspiration Glacier roped up (same crevasse hazard as the approach, and the spot where fog/whiteout has caught parties off guard right at the summit) back to Klawatti Col, then reverse the Eldorado Glacier, Roush Creek basin, boulder field, and climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead. The biggest descent hazard on this route is deteriorating weather/visibility on the open ice cap, not the rock step itself — parties should have a bearing or GPS track for the col-to-glacier-camp leg before committing to the climb.
hazards: open crevasses
bergschrund crossing
rockfall
afternoon snow softening
corniced summit ridge
loose rock on class 4 sections

waysIn.name: Klawatti Col and the south flank to the bergschrund below the face
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Aug once the schrund bridges have consolidated; a separate Apr-Jun window exists for the face as a firm corn-snow line
waysIn.notes:
Identical approach to the SW Buttress as far as the col: Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the Cascade River log crossing, the steep timbered climbers' path, the boulder field (stay climber's right — cairn lines trending left lead into cliffier ground), the basin at 5,500-5,800 ft, then Roush Creek and bivy sites at 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up there.

Climb the Eldorado Glacier, then make the long, mostly flat traverse east and north across the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at about 7,800 ft. Reckon roughly 7-8 miles and over 6,500 ft of gain one way from the car to the foot of the climb, normally split over two or three days.

From the col a short direct climb up the peak's south-facing flank reaches the base. Parties leave the col around 4 a.m. on purpose: this is a south-facing snow slope, icy in the pre-dawn shade and softening fast once the sun is on it, and it is roughly an hour and a half up and an hour down from the col.
hazards: A bergschrund, and later in the season a moat, guarding the base of the face
Several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow directly above the schrund, on ground where a slip does not stop
South aspect: icy before dawn, softening and wet-sliding by mid-morning
Whiteout on the Inspiration Glacier both ways — parties have been caught out right at the summit
A crumbly, elongated summit where the true high point is genuinely hard to identify

name: Standard Route
approach: The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, climbing the snow headwall to the summit ridge and an easy talus-and-ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line. In mid-July the stretch past White Pass to the high camp near 6,600 ft has several unexpected dips and re-climbs of a couple hundred feet, adding time to the day.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following a separate down-route: downclimb the summit talus/ledges and the snow headwall, and re-cross the White River Glacier, Glacier Gap, and White Chuck Glacier back to Foam Basin/White River Meadows camp, then retrace the boot path over White Pass to the PCT/North Fork Sauk Trail junction and down the switchbacks and river-valley trail miles to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are known on this route, and parties describe reversing the glacier-and-ridge line rather than any rope-lowering. The real descent hazards are glacier hazards, not rock hazards: one party found fully open crevasses low on the White Chuck Glacier requiring careful route-finding/crampon work, and a roughly 200-yard section of exposed blue ice (a shallow icefall) on the White River Glacier that demands careful crampon travel; stay roped for glacier travel on the way down as well as up, and expect snow bridges to be less trustworthy and crevasses less obvious in early season than by late summer. Budget real time for the descent — the same party took about 5.3 hours from summit back to camp alone, before the multi-hour trail hike-out. Glissading may be feasible on snow-filled sections for parties comfortable self-arresting, especially early season, but it is an optional shortcut, not a required part of the route.
hazards: open crevasses and sections of blue ice on the White Chuck and White River Glaciers, more exposed later in the season (Aug-Sept)
long, largely off-trail approach (12+ miles one-way) with serious route-finding, especially in the Lightning Creek drainage and on the glaciers themselves
high, fast water at Red Creek and Lightning Creek crossings, especially during early-season snowmelt
dense brush on the lower, effectively unmaintained sections of the White River Trail beyond the Boulder Creek Trail junction
remoteness - many hours/miles from help if injured or benighted, with no reliable cell coverage
access-road washouts and closures on FR 49 / the Mountain Loop Highway that can block the west approach entirely

waysIn.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
waysIn.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier are unreadable under early-season cover
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last stretch off maintained trail: navigation errors cost hours
Road washouts and closures on FR 49 and the Mountain Loop Highway can block this approach
Whiteout and weather exposure on the open glacier plateau; loose talus on the summit scramble
Remote: no cell coverage, self-rescue only

waysIn.name: White River trail from the east
waysIn.notes: From the White River trailhead beyond Lake Wenatchee, walk the White River trail about 10 miles up the valley to the Lightning Creek crossing, then go cross-country up into the high basin east of the peaks. About as far on foot as the Sauk side, with less trail and more off-trail travel.
hazards: Roughly ten miles up the White River valley, the lower sections effectively unmaintained with dense brush
Lightning Creek crossing runs high and fast during snowmelt
Cross-country travel in the Lightning Creek drainage with serious route-finding, little trail
Open crevasses and blue ice on the White River Glacier, more exposed late in the season
Whiteout and weather exposure on the open glacier plateau; loose talus near the summit
Remote: many hours from help, no reliable cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: When approaching from the Lake Wenatchee side, or when the Sauk valley is unavailable; about as far on foot but with less trail and more cross-country travel.

name: Glaciated Scramble (Standard)
approach: From the Blanca Lake Trailhead (elev. ~1,950 ft) at the end of North Fork Skykomish River Road (FR 63), follow Blanca Lake Trail #1052 north into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. The trail starts climbing almost immediately in a long, punishing series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining about 2,900 ft over the first ~3 miles to a ridge crest — this is the steepest, most sustained grind of the whole approach, and can be muddy, rooty, and icy in wet or early-season conditions (microspikes worth carrying outside of high summer). From the ridge the trail rolls on through meadows to Virgin Lake (~4,600 ft, roughly mile 3.5), the high point of the trail; the main tread then drops about 600 ft to Blanca Lake, a good camp for an overnight approach and the last easy, reliable water source before the off-trail climbing begins. For the south-ridge line, do not continue downhill on the main tread toward Blanca Lake at Virgin Lake — that is the way to the Columbia Glacier line described below, and taking it by mistake is the commonest route-finding error here. Instead pick up the faint, unsigned climbers' path leaving the lake into the woods toward Kyes Ridge. This boot path gains Kyes Peak's south ridge and follows it northeast, staying on the ridge's east side to traverse around minor gendarmes; it levels out near 5,300 ft, crosses to the west side around 5,845 ft, then climbs steep heather and scree above, working around cliff bands. A boulder field near 6,300 ft leads to a notch by Point 7026, from which class 3-4 scrambling on so-so Monte Cristo-group rock gains the summit ridge and final block. Total elevation gain from trailhead to the 7,282-ft high point is roughly 6,000 ft over about 6-7 miles one-way (12-14 miles round trip) — this is a long single push with a likely-after-dark return, or better done as an overnight camped at Virgin Lake. An alternative approach/ascent line climbs the Columbia Glacier out of the Blanca Lake basin (low-angled but genuinely crevassed — rope, axe, and crampons are the safe call even though some parties skip them in low-snow years) and gains the upper mountain from the north; several trip reports pair this glacier line for the ascent with the south-ridge climbers' trail for the descent, or the reverse.
descent: The standard descent reverses the south-ridge climbers' trail back down to Virgin Lake and out Blanca Lake Trail #1052 to the trailhead — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent, and there are no fixed anchors or rap stations reported anywhere on the route. That said, the crux comes on the way down, not up: downclimbing the summit block and a short, exposed 4th-class knife-edge section reads noticeably harder in the downhill direction, and the faint climbers' trail below the ridge is easy to lose in the brushy traverse back toward Virgin Lake — budget extra time for route-finding here. Some parties carry a rope and rig a single improvised rappel off a natural anchor (sling around a rock horn or block — no bolts or fixed gear reported) to protect the summit-block downclimb or the knife-edge crux, particularly with a less-experienced party or in wet/icy conditions; treat this as optional protection for one short pitch rather than a required multi-rappel descent, so a single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient if you bring one. Descending via the Columbia Glacier can be faster and more enjoyable than fighting the brushy climbers' trail, conditions permitting (visible, avoidable crevasses and a not-too-broken-up glacier); if you go that way, watch for crevasses on the lower apron and soft, sliding midday slush in summer snow. Whichever line you descend, this is commonly a long day with a probable dark finish, or plan a second night at Virgin Lake.
hazards: long, rugged Monte Cristo approach
glacier travel and crevasses on the Columbia Glacier, especially in soft or late-day snow
routefinding on the upper peak and on the faint Kyes Ridge climber's trail, which is easy to lose
loose, crumbly ('kitty litter') rock on the lateral moraine and summit block
wading or log-crossing the Blanca Lake outlet stream
dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse in late season

waysIn.name: Blanca Lake Trail to Virgin Lake, then the south-ridge climbers' path
waysIn.season: July to October. Early season adds snow on the ridge and makes the glacier variant the safer of the two.
waysIn.notes: From the Blanca Lake trailhead at the end of the North Fork road, follow the lake trail north into the wilderness. It climbs immediately in a long series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining most of the day's easy elevation over the first three miles to a ridge crest — muddy, rooty and icy in wet or early-season conditions. From the ridge the trail runs on through meadows to Virgin Lake, the trail's high point before it drops about six hundred feet to the big lake, and a good overnight camp and the last easy reliable water before the off-trail climbing. This is where the single most common navigation error happens.
hazards: The unsigned turnoff at Virgin Lake is the commonest error on this peak
Route-finding on the faint ridge path, which is easy to lose in brush
Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block with real exposure
Dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse late in the season
A long single push with a likely after-dark return unless camped at the lake

waysIn.name: Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake basin
waysIn.season: July to October. Best when the glacier is snow-covered enough to bridge but firm enough to travel; midday summer slush makes it slow and sliding.
waysIn.notes: The alternative line onto the upper mountain, and several parties pair it with the ridge path — one for the way up, one for the way down. From Virgin Lake, take the main tread down into the basin, cross or skirt the lake's south shore on logs and boulders (poles help), then work up the boulder field and heather slopes above the north shore to the glacier toe. Stay on the glacier's east side; the west-side ice is noticeably steeper.
hazards: Crevasses on the Columbia Glacier — low-angle but real, especially where snow is soft
Soft, sliding midday slush in summer
Wading or log-crossing the lake outlet stream
Loose, crumbly rock on the lateral moraine and at the glacier exit
Camping is banned within half a mile of the big lake, so plan the overnight around Virgin Lake
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the glacier is snow-covered and firm enough to travel, often as the other half of a loop with the ridge path; early season it is the safer choice when the ridge is snowy.

name: East Ridge
approach: From the East Fork Foss River Trailhead (~1,650 ft, reached via a signed spur off US 2 near Skykomish), follow the Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail parallels the East Fork Foss River through old-growth forest, passing established camps and a boot path near mile 4 that drops to the river for water. The trail then crosses the East Fork (log crossing, can be a wet-footed ford or tricky in high water/early season) and turns steep, climbing roughly 2,400 ft in the next 3 miles over large boulders and tree roots on a rugged, minimally maintained tread — the crux of the approach for footing and stamina. This deposits you at Jade Lake (~mile 8, 4,600 ft), the first of the Necklace Valley chain; continue past Emerald Lake (~mile 9, seasonal stream at its north end for water) toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes at the head of the valley under the cliffs of La Bohn Gap, where the maintained trail effectively ends and boot paths fan out. From the Opal Lake camp area, leave the trail and pick up a crude, unmaintained boot path climbing 'La Bohn Creek,' the outlet stream of La Bohn Lakes — a steep, west-facing, often hot and exposed slog with no reliable shade. This path eases at the lowest La Bohn Lake; continue north along the lakeshore/heather benches to the upper lake, then make a short talus/heather traverse east to the broad 5,900-ft saddle of La Bohn Gap (note: USGS maps mislabel the gap roughly 2/3 mile southeast of its true position — verify you're at the correct broad saddle before committing to slopes east of it, which end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena). From the gap, head west up boulders and heather onto the east ridge and follow it, over a false summit and a short, blocky knife-edge, to La Bohn Peak's summit (6,585 ft); stay off the north side of the summit block, which drops away in a cliff. An alternative that avoids losing/regaining elevation is to leave the main trail near Tank Lakes and follow the 'Magic Staircase' — a bench around 5,200–5,400 ft on La Bohn Peak's south side — over to Chain Lakes and then up to La Bohn Gap from the south. Total one-way distance to the summit is roughly 9–10 miles from the trailhead with about 5,000 ft of cumulative gain; this is realistically a 2-3 day backpack for most parties rather than a car-to-car push. Water is reliable along the East Fork Foss and at the Necklace Valley lakes but scarce above La Bohn Lakes.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved. Descend the same east ridge and its talus back down to La Bohn Gap, watching footing on loose, occasionally wobbly boulders (parties describe roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders, some that wobble, on this face). From the gap, reverse the boot path down the steep La Bohn Creek drainage to the La Bohn Lakes and back into Necklace Valley, then rejoin the Necklace Valley Trail #1062 for the long descent back through the boulder/root section to Jade Lake and out along the East Fork Foss River to the trailhead. Parties wanting to avoid re-losing and re-gaining elevation at the gap can instead descend south from the gap to Chain Lakes and take the 'Magic Staircase' bench (~5,200–5,400 ft) back toward Tank Lakes before dropping into Necklace Valley — a reasonable variation but not shorter, mainly smoother underfoot. Key hazards on descent are the same as on ascent in reverse: loose/unstable talus on the peak's flank, potential lingering snow patches on the upper slopes into early summer (which can mask the correct gap location — the true La Bohn Gap is commonly misidentified from the USGS map, and dropping east of the wrong 'gap' leads onto cliffs above Lake Rowena), and the steep, exposed, often-hot boot path down the La Bohn Creek drainage, which is unpleasant and slick if wet. The East Fork Foss River crossing partway down should be treated with the same caution as on the approach.
hazards: loose talus and scree on the final ~1,000 ft above La Bohn Gap
snow/ice can linger in the summit gully/chimney into August
cliff band and exposure on the north side of the summit block — easy to wander too far north, especially in fog
afternoon thunderstorms common in late summer
unmaintained, steep boot path up the La Bohn Creek drainage between Necklace Valley and La Bohn Lakes — route-finding and loose footing
foot-log crossing of the East Fork Foss River near mile 5 can feel exposed with high snowmelt

waysIn.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Creek to the gap
waysIn.season: Late July to September
waysIn.notes: The first five miles of the Necklace Valley Trail are nearly flat along the river; save your legs, because everything above the log crossing of the East Fork Foss is steep. Roughly 2,400 ft of gain in three miles over large boulders and tree roots on rugged tread brings you to Jade Lake, then it is up-valley past Emerald toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes where the maintained trail effectively ends. From the Opal Lake camps pick up the crude path climbing beside La Bohn Creek — west-facing, unshaded and hot in the afternoon — to the lowest La Bohn Lake, then follow the shore and heather benches north to the upper lake.
hazards: Roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders on the peak's flank, many of which wobble
Steep, unshaded and slick-when-wet boot path up the La Bohn Creek drainage
Foot-log crossing of the East Fork Foss at high snowmelt
Snow lingering on the upper slopes that masks the correct saddle
Cliffs above Lake Rowena on the ground east of the wrong gap

name: Northern Aspect
approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount (paved for roughly the first third, then gravel, narrow and steep near the end) 23.1 miles to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (road-end elevation about 3,660 ft). Hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles / 1,700 ft gain to Cascade Pass, then continue cross-country/on climbers' path south on the Ptarmigan Traverse: ascend the Cache Glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), descend to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), cross the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier, climb to the Spider-Formidable col (~7,300 ft), and descend to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft), which serves as the standard base camp below Le Conte's north side. This approach alone is a full day of glacier travel with sustained elevation gain and loss.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the exposed ledge traverse and loose rock back to the rock outcropping below the North Face, then descend the east-slope talus and snow to bypass Peak 7004, returning to the Yang Yang Lakes camp. From camp, retrace the Ptarmigan Traverse route: recross the Middle Cascade Glacier, climb back up to Kool-Aid Lake, ascend to Cache Col, and descend the Cache Glacier to Cascade Pass, then hike the maintained Cascade Pass Trail back to the trailhead. Parties commonly camp at Yang Yang Lakes or Pelton Basin/Cascade Pass on the way out rather than exiting in a single push.
hazards: Glacier crevasse hazard on the Cache Glacier and Middle Cascade Glacier sections of the approach.
Loose rock on the summit ledge traverse and on the east-slope talus below Peak 7004.
Snow conditions on the approach can be firm/icy early season and soft/sketchy late season, both requiring axe and crampon competence.

waysIn.name: Yang Yang Lakes, the secret stair, and the outcrop under the north face
waysIn.season: Late Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: From camp between the Yang Yang Lakes, pass the southern tip of the southernmost lake, walk on about 900 ft, then turn sharply right onto a bearing of roughly 320 degrees. Two ways gain the ridgeline from here and neither is wrong on its own terms: a clear but very steep boot pack to the left up a gully, and a mixed snow, dirt and talus ridge to the right. Take the gully when there is snow in it and the dirt ridge when there is not — using the gully dry, or the dirt ridge under snow, is the mistake. This is the most difficult and consequential piece of the whole leg. Above it the route follows the ridge south around forested ground and up talus.
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard just to reach the camp
The precipitous compacted-dirt path of the secret stair
Tedious loose talus on Peak 7004's east slope when the snow has gone
An exposed traverse of narrow, loose ledges near the top, on a summit with very little standing room

name: Leche La Vaca
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599): gentle forest walking along Mountaineer Creek for 1.5 miles to a log-bridge crossing, then left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a final boulder-moraine push to the lake outlet — about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, 2.5-3 hours. Top off water here, the last reliable source. Continue around toward the lake's south/east shore onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining steep talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; a slope that holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips). Cut climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a dense slide-alder/heather band (15-20 minutes of real bushwhacking) to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Leche La Vaca starts in this same base gully area on the left side of the wall, near Scarface; the final approach scramble to the wall is loose 3rd/4th class terrain. Figure 3.5-4 hours car-to-base overall.
descent: Leche La Vaca's fifth pitch, a long 4th-class to low-5th traverse, ends at the summit block — from there it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard walk-off: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (staying off the balanced boulder itself) down to a broad sandy scree/talus gully, descending clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short step near the top of this descent is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side rather than downclimbing it — treat this as optional, not mandatory. No full rappel of the route itself is required.
hazards: Loose rock and party-induced rockfall, particularly on the easy upper terrain and the walk-off.
Full exposure to fast-building afternoon thunderstorms on the summit ridge.
Snow lingers on the descent slopes into July and returns in October.
The west aspect keeps the wall shaded and cold through the morning; early-season verglas is possible on the lower pitches.

name: East Route (Main Peak)
approach: Start at the Pete Lake Trailhead (aka Cooper Lake / Cooper River trailhead, ~2,800') on FR 4616 off Cooper Lake Road (FS-46); a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Follow the Cooper River Trail (Trail #1323) roughly 4 flat, forested miles to Pete Lake (~2,980'). Continue along the lakeshore and past its camps for about another 1.2 miles, staying right at the first fork rather than crossing the creek, to reach the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Turn south (left) on the PCT for about 0.8 mile to the Lemah Creek crossing. Leave the maintained trail near the Lemah Creek crossing (the PCT bridge here washed out years ago and has not been replaced; parties ford or cross on logs) and head west/cross-country toward Upper Lemah Meadows — an intermittent climbers' path and sparse cairns mark the way for the first ~1,000 feet before fading into open terrain. From there it's another 1-2 miles of off-trail travel up the Lemah Creek valley — past small waterfalls and swimming holes, through several creek crossings, and some brushy slide-alder sections — gaining to a meadow camp around 3,600'. Most parties camp here or continue up the valley along the creek to about 5,000' where the glacier remnant/snowfinger terminates. From there climb to roughly 6,200' and exit left (south) up a short cliff step onto the glacial remnants/snowfields on the peak's southeast side. Traverse to just southwest of the main summit and climb a series of Class 2-3 cliff bands to the col between Lemah Two and the Main (East) Peak — this is the technical crux of the approach/climb and the point most trip reports flag for route-finding and loose rock. Total is roughly 16 miles round trip with ~4,700' of gain, and parties commonly take 8-10+ hours from trailhead to summit, so many split it into a two-day trip with a camp near 3,600'. Hazards: cold, sometimes thigh-deep early-season creek crossings on Lemah Creek; brush and downed timber off-trail; loose, exposed Class 2-3 scrambling in the cliff bands; and a genuine route-finding crux locating the correct gully/cliff-band line up to the col, especially in fog, low visibility, or lingering snow.
descent: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent line: down from the summit block via the NW ridge to just below the true summit, back down through the col between Lemah Two and Lemah Main, down the Class 2-3 cliff bands, across the southeast snowfields/glacial remnants, and back down the valley to camp and out the same cross-country/PCT/Pete Lake Trail approach. This is not a walk-off in the sense of a maintained trail all the way — expect the same off-trail, brushy, creek-crossing travel in reverse. On the technical section near the col/notch (above ~7,200'), many parties downclimb the Class 3-4 rock and short snow/ice moat, but a documented descent used rappels here instead of downclimbing the more exposed step: that party rigged for four rappel stations but ended up doing three (having passed the first anchor), with a 60m rope reaching a small ledge/platform from which the remaining short section was downclimbed. Anchors on this section are natural — slings around rock horns/chockstones, not bolted or fixed gear — so bring cordage/slings and be prepared to build your own. Bring a 60m rope (or a 30m single is enough for some parties who downclimb more and rappel less); carrying less rope means more downclimbing of exposed 3rd/4th-class terrain. Descent hazards: rockfall in the gully/cliff-band system (especially with multiple parties on route), a snow/ice moat near the top of the gully that can be tricky to negotiate depending on season, and losing the correct downclimbing line through the cliff bands, which can cliff you out onto steeper terrain. Given the long round-trip time, plan for the possibility of finishing the hike-out in the dark.
hazards: loose rock
exposed summit step
multiple confusing summits (USGS quads have historically mislabeled the high point)
Lemah Creek ford on approach
glacier travel and moat crossings near the rock step
route-finding through brush and cliff bands below the glacier

waysIn.name: Pete Lake and the PCT, leaving the trail at the Lemah Creek footbridge
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the chute below the summit is easier as snow than as loose rock, so earlier is often better
waysIn.notes: Walk the Cooper River trail #1323 about four flat miles to Pete Lake, then roughly another mile and a quarter past the lake, staying right at the first fork rather than crossing the creek, to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn left (south) on the PCT and follow it about 0.8 mile to Lemah Creek. The trail-leaving cue is sharp: leave the trail where it reaches Lemah Creek, at the site of the washed-out PCT bridge, where there is a campsite. If you have crossed the creek you have gone past it. A faint path climbs the creek side past waterfalls — Whinnimic Falls is the big one — and within about twenty minutes the ground opens onto rocky knobs. The valley floor above is flat and marshy at around 3,700 ft. Continue roughly a mile and more up the valley to the marshy basin under the long snow gully that starts on the north side of Lemah Five. Two lines lead from that basin up to the Lemah Glacier and neither is obvious from the marsh; one of them carries significant brush. Where the gully melts out at a waterfall, it is better to stay right and return to snow above than to scramble the left side. Leave the gully onto heather around 4,800 ft. One further note on names: Lemah has five summits and the main one is the middle, Lemah Three. Lemah Two is a different top on the same ridge.
hazards: Cold, sometimes thigh-deep creek crossings in the Lemah valley early season
Brush and blowdown on an unmaintained, lightly-used path
The moat beside the rock step
Loose rock on the final hundred feet if you take the gully rather than the ridge
Very poor rock quality generally — this ridge is chossy even by Cascade standards

name: Let it Burn
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — forest along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain). Fill water here — it's the last source. Cross the outlet and continue toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake, then cut left through dense brush to the obvious base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the gully, scramble up a 3rd-class ramp to the actual base of the technical climbing. A documented approach for this route took about 3 hours 47 minutes trailhead-to-base, matching the 3.5-4 hour estimate.
descent: From the top of the route, most parties make an optional ~30m rappel down the south/southwest side off a slung horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — this step can be bypassed entirely if the party avoids the summit block area. After the rappel (or bypass), descend scree or snow rightward (clockwise around the peak) back to the base of the climb. A documented descent took about 50 minutes from the top of the route to the base, plus roughly 3 hours 5 minutes hiking back out to the trailhead. This is the same walk-off shared by the West Face and The Scoop. Loose rock on the scree gully is the main hazard, especially with parties above; watch footing on wet or snow-covered sections early in the season.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the formation

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet below the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
Loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final scramble to the wall
Loose basin talus
Long dry stretch above the lake

waysIn.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
waysIn.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band — a real bushwhack
Loose gully talus; snow lingering in the gully into early summer
Cairns stop at the base of the gully
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the outlet at the lake's north end is awkward to cross, or when you want to come in from the Aasgard side by the gully; longer, with a short bushwhack through alder.

name: East Face
approach: Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass (a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond). The climbers' path starts just left (west) of the highway's east-side guardrail/barrier and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest. It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes (some parties report closer to an hour) of steep hiking/scrambling from the pullout to the base of the wall, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. There are two common ways to gain the actual start depending on snow coverage: a gully/snowfield left of the face, or scrambling in from climber's right on rock. Early-to-mid season the approach gully can hold firm snow well into summer (ice axe/traction useful); by late August it is typically dry talus and easily avoided. No reliable water source on this short approach — carry what you need from the car.
descent: The standard descent is a walk-off, not a rappel-the-face descent. From the notch below the true summit (not the summit itself), head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left — roughly 20 feet of 3rd-class terrain. Old rap slings are present in this gully but most parties simply downclimb rather than bother rigging a rappel. From the base of the gully, traverse right (north) until you intersect the well-worn climbers'/cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to join the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road-walking versus following Blue Lake Trail all the way to its own trailhead. Some parties instead choose to rappel directly back down the East Face route itself (useful in bad weather or if the walk-off is unfamiliar/snow-covered) — one documented descent of the face took 7 double-rope (60m) rappels, built from a mix of slung horns/rap rings and a couple of fixed/bolted anchors encountered on route. That face-rappel line is not the recommended standard descent, just an alternative to the normal walk-off descent.
hazards: A snowfield lingers at the base early season, affecting how you gain the rock.
Offwidth and chimney sections are strenuous and can feel committing.
You do not tag the true summit; the descent gully has loose third-class downclimbing.

waysIn.name: The hairpin pond pullout, the steep forest path, and the treed ledge below the east face
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20 about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass, a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond. The climbers' path starts just left, west, of the highway's east-side guardrail and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest.

It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes, some parties closer to an hour, of steep hiking and scrambling from the pullout to the base, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. No water; carry what you need from the car.
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
A 5.8 pitch as one of the two ways to gain the base
Snow lingering in the talus into early-mid summer
No water on the approach
A descent that finishes at the Blue Lake Trail, not at the pond pullout
